summary: A conifer native to coastal California and south-western Oregon that produces the tallest living trees on Earth. Some coast redwoods have reached about 2,000 years old, and coastal fog supplies an important part of their water.

A deciduous shrub native to the Mediterranean in southern Europe, southwest Asia and northwest Africa. Its grey-green, rush-like shoots bear very sparse leaves and abundant fragrant yellow flowers; the black seed pods later burst with an audible crack.
edibilityNote: The plant is used as a flavoring, although alkaloids in all parts have toxic effects.

summary: Perennial flowering herb native to temperate Eurasia and North Africa. Its clustered yellow pea-like flowers produce pods whose arrangement resembles a bird’s foot, while its five leaflets appear trefoil-like because three sit conspicuously above the other two.

A flowering shrub or small tree native to Bolivia, it has spreading stems and auburn or reddish, densely hairy new growth. Raspberry-like buds open into rounded powder-puff flower heads formed by numerous prominent red stamens, though white-flowered plants also occur.
A deciduous tree native to southwestern and eastern Asia. Its many small leaflets slowly close at night and during rain, while its summer flowers resemble starbursts of silky pink threads.
edibilityNote: The flowers are reportedly used to make teas and are described as psychoactive.

summary: A small, fast-growing tree native to southern Mexico, Belize and Guatemala. It has thornless branches, cream-coloured flower puffs and flat seed pods, and can form dense thickets outside its native range.
edibilityNote: Young pods are eaten in parts of Indonesia, Laos and Thailand; seeds contain toxic mimosine, and cooking is thought to remove most poison.

summary: Deciduous bramble shrub native to the west coast of North America. Its prickly stems form thickets, and its raspberry-like fruit is yellow-orange or red. The fruit is eaten raw or processed, while Indigenous peoples traditionally ate young shoots, usually peeled and cooked before they became woody.
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten raw or processed into preserves, candy and wine; Indigenous peoples also ate peeled young shoots, usually cooked before becoming woody.

summary: A coniferous woodland tree native across much of Europe and parts of western Asia, the Caucasus and northwestern Africa. It has flat dark-green leaves and bright-red, berry-like arils surrounding its seeds; every part except the fleshy aril is poisonous.
edibilityNote: Only the fleshy red aril is edible; some foragers eat it, but the enclosed seed and all other parts are poisonous.

summary: A large evergreen conifer endemic to Gran Canaria, Tenerife, El Hierro and La Palma in the Canary Islands. It bears long, often drooping needles in bundles of three and glossy brown cones that may stay closed for years. In its native area, lower-trunk shoots with single bluish-green juvenile leaves appear only after fire or other damage, and trees can resprout after fire.

Deciduous tree native to Europe, southwest and central Asia, and northwest Africa. Black poplar has diamond-shaped to triangular green leaves and grows rapidly in open, low-lying areas with moist ground.

Deciduous tree native from North Africa’s Atlas Mountains through southern and central Europe into Central Asia. Young bark is pale with distinctive dark diamond marks, becoming blackish and deeply cracked near the base with age. Root suckers can spread far from the trunk and form extensive colonies.

A deciduous tree native to cool temperate Europe and Asia, European aspen has nearly round, coarsely toothed adult leaves that tremble on flattened stalks. It spreads extensively through root sprouts, forming large clonal colonies.

Juniper shrub native to the mountains of central and southern Europe and western and central Asia. Mature plants carry scale-like leaves, sometimes retaining juvenile needle-like leaves, especially on shaded lower shoots. Its berry-like cones are blue-black with a whitish waxy coating.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous because they contain toxic compounds, including ethereal oils.

summary: A low-growing shrub native to northern North America, across most of Canada and parts of the northern United States. It spreads several metres while staying close to the ground, with scale-like adult leaves and dark-blue, wax-coated, berry-like cones.

A herbaceous perennial flowering plant native to Eurasia, the common dandelion has yellow flower heads that become round balls of silver-tufted fruit dispersed by wind. Its leaves, flowers and roots are sometimes used as food: leaves raw or cooked, flowers in wine, and baked, ground roots as a coffee substitute.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw or cooked; flowers are used for wine; baked, ground roots have served as a coffee substitute.

summary: A herbaceous annual, or biennial in warm climates, native to Macaronesia, temperate Eurasia, and northern and northeastern Africa. Its long, stork-bill-shaped seed pods burst open in spirals, and the moisture-responsive seeds can move across the ground and drill into crevices. Young leaves are eaten raw or cooked; the whole young plant is reportedly edible and tastes like sharp parsley.
edibilityNote: Young leaves are edible raw or cooked; the whole plant is reportedly edible when young, with a sharp parsley-like flavour.

summary: An annual flowering plant widespread across most of Europe, northern Africa, southwest and central Asia, and Macaronesia. Its square stems carry whorls of rough, bristly leaves, while tiny pale lilac or pink flowers appear in small clusters.

summary: A perennial herb native to eastern North American woodlands. Its upright stems carry deeply divided, toothed leaves and rose-purple to violet flowers in spring or early summer. The ripe fruit springs open, with five seed cells joined to a long beak-like column.

Fast-growing, short-lived tree native to North America from Canada to Honduras. Unlike most maples, it regularly has compound leaves with more than three leaflets, and male and female flowers grow on separate trees. Native American peoples made syrup from its sap and prepared the inner bark as winter food or crystallized sugar.
edibilityNote: Native American peoples made syrup and drinks from the sap and prepared inner bark as winter food or crystallized sugar.

summary: A perennial, spore-producing horsetail found across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, commonly forming dense colonies beside or within still or slow freshwater. Its green, jointed stems are mostly hollow and spread mainly through underground stems. Early spring shoots were historically eaten, including as a vegetable by poorer Romans, despite being unpalatable and not nutritious.
edibilityNote: Early spring shoots were historically eaten; poorer Romans sometimes used them as a vegetable despite their poor taste and low nutritional value.

summary: Herbaceous flowering perennial native to Europe, western Asia and northwest Africa, yellow iris has bright yellow flowers and erect, sword-like leaves. It thrives in very wet places and spreads quickly by rhizomes and water-carried seeds.
edibilityNote: The roots and leaves are toxic.

summary: Short-trunked or trunkless yucca native to deserts of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. It has blue-green leaves and white-to-cream spring flowers tinged purple, followed by banana-shaped fruit eaten raw or cooked; young flower stalks are cooked after their tough rind is removed.
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten raw or cooked and was historically dried for winter; young flower stalks are cooked after peeling, and flowers are also eaten.

summary: A semi-evergreen oak native to the California Floristic Province, coast live oak keeps living leaves year-round and often develops a massive, gnarled trunk with age. Many Indigenous Californians still forage its acorns for food when available, especially for special events.
edibilityNote: Many Indigenous Californians still forage the acorns for food when available, especially for special events.

summary: A large annual native to the Himalayas, specifically between Kashmir and Uttarakhand. It has hooded pink flowers and seed pods that explode when disturbed, and it is invasive across many areas of the Northern Hemisphere.
edibilityNote: Nectar, green seed pods, seeds, young leaves and shoots are edible; flowers are made into jam or parfait. Eat in moderation because of oxalates.

summary: A low-growing perennial cactus native to the eastern United States and naturally occurring in southern Ontario, it has flattened green stem segments with barbed bristles and sometimes longer spines. Its yellow or gold flowers are followed by juicy red or purple edible fruits; the fruits require care because of small spiny bristles.
edibilityNote: Fruits, roasted seeds and cooked young segments are edible; spiny bristles or spines must be removed or avoided.

summary: A large cactus native to subtropical and tropical coastal areas of the Americas, especially the Caribbean and lower East Coast of the United States. It has flattened blue-green sections with yellow spines and produces yellow flowers in spring and summer, followed by purple-red fruits.
edibilityNote: The mucilage inside the leaves is edible in the same way as the fruits.

summary: A perennial milkweed native to eastern and southwestern North America. It bears clusters of orange, yellow or red flowers from April to September and has hairy stems that do not release milky sap when broken.
edibilityNote: Native Americans and European pioneers ate young seed pods after boiling them in several changes of water; the plant also contains toxic steroids.

summary: A wetland perennial native to North America and northern South America, broadleaf arrowhead forms crowded colonies linked by runners. Its starchy tubers were important foods for Indigenous peoples of the Americas and can be eaten raw, cooked, or dried into flour.
edibilityNote: Starchy tubers were historically eaten by Native Americans; they may be eaten raw, cooked, or sliced and dried into flour.

summary: A widespread deciduous tree native to eastern and central North America. Its flowers, twigs, leaf stalks and seeds show varying amounts of red, while its autumn leaves can become brilliant deep scarlet. Its sap makes maple syrup, but it must be tapped before the buds emerge, giving a short season.
edibilityNote: Sap is made into maple syrup but must be tapped before the early-emerging buds open.

summary: An herb native to South America, it has opposite, toothed leaves and small flower heads with white outer florets around yellow centres. In Colombia and Oaxaca it is used in soups; it can also go in leaf salads, while in eastern Africa its wild-collected leaves, stems and flowers are eaten or dried and powdered for soup.
edibilityNote: Used in Colombian and Oaxacan soups and leaf salads; in eastern Africa, leaves, stems and flowers are eaten or dried for soup.

summary: A perennial herb native to the cool temperate Northern Hemisphere, especially Asia and Europe. It spreads by underground stems to form extensive colonies and bears clusters of flowers. All parts, including the red berries, are highly poisonous if swallowed, even in small amounts.
edibilityNote: All parts, including the red berries, are highly toxic if ingested, even in small quantities.

summary: Evergreen shrub or small tree native to Madeira, formerly present in the Canary Islands and introduced in the Azores. It has dense glossy foliage and fragrant white flowers resembling lily of the valley. The plant contains andromedotoxin and is toxic to humans.
edibilityNote: The plant contains andromedotoxin and is toxic to humans, potentially causing diarrhoea or sudden death.

summary: Annual or perennial flowering plant native to the United States and Mexico. Its silky, four-petalled flowers appear in brilliant yellow, orange or red, occasionally pink or white, and close at night or during cold, windy weather. The fruit may split with an audible snap to scatter its seeds.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten or used as garnish, while the seeds are used in cooking.

summary: Perennial flowering herb native to Europe, Asia and northwestern Africa. Its creeping stems root at their joints to form new plants, while its leaves may have variable pale markings and its flowers are glossy yellow. The plant is poisonous, although its poisons are lost when dried in hay.
edibilityNote: The plant is poisonous when fresh, although its poisons are lost when dried in hay.

summary: An evergreen fern native to parts of tropical Africa, the western Indian Ocean, Asia, eastern Australia and many Pacific islands. It forms small underground tubers and upright, feather-like fronds, and has become invasive in some introduced areas, including Florida.

A large coniferous tree native to the Pacific Northwest of North America. Exceptionally long-lived, it has flat sprays of scale-like leaves that smell strongly of pineapple when crushed, and aromatic, decay-resistant wood of major cultural importance to Indigenous peoples.
edibilityNote: Pacific Northwest First Nations regarded the tree as providing food, though the passage gives no plant part or preparation.

summary: Conifer native to western North America. Its coastal variety ranges from central-western British Columbia south to central California, with a continuous range from the Cascade Range to the Pacific coast in Oregon and Washington.

A perennial flowering shrub or small tree native to the Americas, it bears clusters of showy golden-yellow trumpet-shaped flowers. It readily colonizes disturbed ground and can form dense invasive thickets outside its native range.
edibilityNote: The plant itself is described as nontoxic, but honey made from its flowers is poisonous.

summary: A perennial climbing vine native to Mexico’s Atlantic and Pacific coastal plains. It has large heart-shaped leaves and showy, usually pink flowers that may bloom throughout the year. Its tubers and seeds are edible; Indigenous inhabitants of Baja California Sur historically toasted and ground the seeds or boiled them for fried cakes.
edibilityNote: Tubers and seeds are edible; Baja California Sur’s Indigenous inhabitants historically toasted and ground seeds or boiled them for fried cakes.

summary: Perennial herb native to Arizona, New Mexico and northern Mexico. Its deep pink to red flowers are sweetly fragrant and bell-shaped, and attract bees and hummingbirds.
Deciduous fern native to moist forests in eastern North America. It has fine, frilly fronds on curved reddish-brown to shining black stems, and its new coiled fronds emerge pink in spring.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native to eastern North America from southern Michigan to central Mexico, eastern redbud bears clusters of magenta-pink flowers on bare branches and sometimes directly on its trunk. Its leaves are heart-shaped, and its fruits are flat, pea-like pods.
edibilityNote: Flowers are eaten fresh, fried, raw or boiled; Native Americans also eat roasted seeds. Southern Appalachian green-twig seasoning is reported with an uncited claim.

summary: A flowering plant native to northern South America and southwestern North America. Its many cultivated forms produce berries ranging from sweet bell peppers to intensely hot chillies. Domesticated in Mexico around 6,000 years ago, the fruits are eaten fresh, dried, pickled or powdered.
edibilityNote: The fruits are consumed fresh, dried, pickled or powdered; wild peppers may have been eaten more than 8,000 years ago.

summary: A deciduous shrub native to North America, it spreads by rhizomes and can form dense thickets. It produces pink bell-shaped flowers and fleshy white berry-like fruits, but the fruit and shrub are poisonous to humans and cause vomiting.
edibilityNote: The fruit and shrub are poisonous to humans and can cause vomiting.

summary: Deciduous leguminous shrub native to western and central Europe. Its ridged green stems become covered with golden-yellow flowers, followed by black pods that burst open audibly and throw their seeds; it contains toxic alkaloids affecting the heart and nervous system.

Large herbaceous perennial native to eastern North America, the Midwest and the South. It has red-to-purple stems and dark berries, but all parts can be toxic; only young shoots and leaves—not roots—are edible after repeated boiling, while mature leaves, stems and berries are poisonous.
edibilityNote: Young leaves and shoots are traditional Appalachian food only after repeated boiling; roots, mature leaves and stems, and berries are poisonous.

summary: An annual herb or short-lived shrubby perennial with strongly scented, hollow green or purple-black stems. Its fragrant trumpet-shaped flowers vary widely in colour and may be single, double or triple, while the seed capsules bear warts or short, sparse spines.
edibilityNote: All parts contain highly poisonous tropane alkaloids and may be fatal if ingested by humans.

summary: A herb native to Europe and southwestern Central Asia, catnip has whitish hairs on its leaves and stems and purple or white, red-speckled flowers. It excites many domestic and large cats. In Roman-era Europe it was valued as tea; its leaves later seasoned meat, sauces and soups.
edibilityNote: Historically used as tea in Roman-era Europe; leaves seasoned meat in the Middle Ages and sauces and soups in France.

summary: Herbaceous perennial wildflower originally native to grasslands from Kansas and Missouri west to northeastern New Mexico and Texas. Its fragrant, cup-shaped flowers open white and turn shell-pink as they age. They typically bloom before dawn and close in full sun.

A herbaceous perennial native to parts of eastern North America, purple coneflower grows in dry open woods, prairies and barrens. Its prominent domed flower heads are usually, but not always, purple in the wild and attract bees and butterflies.
A flowering plant native to Mexico, Central America and northern South America. Its flowers occur in vivid shades of yellow, orange and red, and attract birds and butterflies, including monarchs.
edibilityNote: Young shoots are eaten raw or cooked in west Java; flowers are consumed in Thai salads or herbal tea.

summary: A flowering plant native to the eastern United States and Canada. Its summer flowers are tiny and pink, packed into narrow, tapering clusters, while the stems and leaf undersides carry dense white woolly hairs.

A perennial wetland plant native across most of Eurasia and North America, and more locally in Africa and South America. Its adjoining male and female flower sections develop into the familiar brown, sausage-shaped seed head, which persists through winter before breaking apart in spring.
edibilityNote: Rhizomes require cooking and skinning; peeled stems and leaf bases may be raw or cooked. Young spikes, shoots and sprouts are edible; avoid polluted or bitter specimens.

summary: An annual grass native to Europe and now a common weed worldwide. Its flower head is a stiff, often yellow-tinged cylinder with short blunt bristles, while sparse hairs near the leaf collar help distinguish it from Setaria viridis.

A perennial plant native to the tallgrass prairies of the central United States. Its dense pink to purplish-pink flower spikes bloom from the top downward in late summer, while pointed, backward-curving bracts distinguish it from similar species.

A coniferous tree native to eastern North America. It can live for more than 500 years and tolerates deep shade, moist soil and slopes. Much of its range is threatened by the invasive hemlock woolly adelgid, which can eventually kill the trees.
edibilityNote: Tea has historically been made from leafy twigs or needles; the inner bark can be eaten raw or boiled and made into flour.

summary: A large evergreen fruit tree native from Pakistan to Malesia, probably originating around western Indo-Burma. Its irregularly shaped fruit has bright orange flesh surrounding a large, flat stone. Unripe mangoes are used for pickles and chutneys, while ripe mangoes are widely eaten as fruit.
edibilityNote: Unripe mangoes are used in pickles and chutneys; ripe mangoes are widely eaten as fruit.

summary: An annual or short-lived perennial flowering plant found from Florida and Texas into Mexico and on various islands in arid lowlands. Its stems end in coiled flower clusters, and it tolerates rocky or sandy soil.

An evergreen conifer tree or shrub native to western North America, from coastal shores to dry mountain and subalpine forests. Many Rocky Mountain populations have cones that remain closed until exposed to high temperatures, while coastal and inland Pacific subspecies typically do not.
edibilityNote: Native Americans ate the inner bark to prevent starvation; cambium edibility depended on its thickness, consistency and sweetness.

summary: Herbaceous perennial native from south-central France and the eastern Pyrenees to north-eastern Spain and the Balearic Islands. Its two-lipped flowers resemble mouths that snap open when squeezed, while its egg-shaped fruit capsules resemble skulls.

An oak tree native to eastern and central North America, it is recognizable by bark ridges with shiny stripes extending down the trunk. Its bitter acorns can be shelled and leached, then eaten whole or ground into meal.
edibilityNote: Acorns can be shelled, tied in cloth and leached to remove bitterness, then eaten whole or ground into meal.

summary: An oak tree native and widespread in eastern and central North America. Its deeply cut, bristle-tipped leaves and velvety white-haired buds aid identification, while its inner bark historically supplied a yellow-orange textile dye.
Deciduous shrub native to China, noted for strongly scented, hanging flowers borne on bare stems in winter. The flowers are yellow to pale green-yellow, usually with purplish-red inner parts.
A herbaceous perennial native to Europe and Asia. It favours wet places and can survive submerged or form floating rafts; its flowers open from pink buds and become blue with yellow centres.

A perennial herb native to the Canary Islands, it has been introduced elsewhere, including the western United States. Its largest oval leaves cluster near the woody stem base, and its tiny hairy flowers form a curved arrangement with flat pink or blue faces.

An evergreen perennial native to South Africa’s Cape Provinces and KwaZulu-Natal, bird of paradise is prized for dramatic flowers resembling a bird’s head. Orange sepals and purplish-blue or white petals emerge one at a time from a hard, beak-like sheath above a fan-shaped crown of leaves.

Deciduous chestnut tree native to China, Taiwan and Korea, though millennia of cultivation obscure its exact original range. Its spiny fruit cases contain two or three glossy brown nuts. The sweet, edible nuts are widely cultivated for food in eastern Asia.
edibilityNote: The sweet nuts are edible, including roasted, and more than 300 cultivars have been selected for nut production.

summary: A creeping succulent native to coastal North Africa and Sinai, the Levant, maritime southern Europe, and several Mediterranean and North Atlantic islands. Glistening water-filled cells cover the plant, and its many-petalled flowers open by morning and close at night. The leaves and seeds are edible; the plant has been promoted and commercially grown as a vegetable.
edibilityNote: Leaves and seeds are edible; it was formerly promoted as a spinach-like vegetable and is now sold commercially in Japan.

summary: Creeping, mat-forming succulent native to South Africa. Its dull-green or yellow-green leaves may age pink, and its yellow flowers open in bright morning sunlight and close at night. Its fruit and leaves are edible; South African ripe fruit are reportedly eaten fresh or made into tart jam, although that detail is marked as needing a citation.
edibilityNote: Fruit and leaves are edible; South African ripe-fruit use fresh or in tart jam is reported but marked as needing a citation.

summary: A large perennial sedge reported as native to western, central and southern Europe, it forms dense tufts in damp woodland, hedges and streamside ground. Its flowers hang in long, catkin-like spikes.

A rare evergreen conifer known in the wild from remote canyons of Wollemi National Park in New South Wales, Australia, the Wollemi pine has dark, knobbly bark and often forms multiple trunks. Nearly all side branches remain unbranched and eventually end in a cone or stop growing and die.

An evergreen shrub native to the eastern United States, mountain laurel bears clustered, five-sided flowers from light pink to white. Its stamens can spring outward and fling pollen onto visiting insects. All parts are poisonous.
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic if eaten; even honey made from its pollen can cause neurological and digestive symptoms in humans.

summary: An evergreen conifer native to eastern North America, eastern redcedar has reddish-brown bark that peels in narrow strips. Young growth bears sharp, needle-like leaves, while adult growth has scale-like leaves; its dark purple-blue, berry-like cones often appear sky-blue under a waxy coating.

A lily native to China, Japan, Korea and the Russian Far East. It has showy orange-and-black, scentless flowers and produces small bulbs in its leaf joints that can grow into cloned plants. In Asia, its bulbs are cultivated and gathered from the wild for food; in Taiwan, the flowers are also eaten.
edibilityNote: Bulbs are cultivated and wild-foraged for food in Asia; both flowers and bulbs are eaten in Taiwan.

summary: Flowering plant native to much of Mexico, Bermuda, the Bahamas, Central and South America, and the Caribbean. It grows on large trees, especially live oaks and bald cypresses in the southeastern United States.

A deciduous tree native to eastern North America and the tropical mountain regions of Mexico and Central America. It is easily remembered by its glossy, star-shaped leaves and hard, round, densely spiked fruits. The leaves often turn vivid yellow, orange, red and purple in autumn, though southern trees may show little colour.
edibilityNote: Gum resin exuded from wounded bark was used to make chewing gum.

summary: A massive, long-lived tree native to the eastern and central United States, northeastern Mexico and extreme southern Canada, the American sycamore favours wetlands and riversides. Its bark flakes away in large irregular pieces, creating a mottled surface of gray, greenish-white and brown.

An evergreen or semi-evergreen conifer tree primarily native to Mexico and Guatemala, with a few populations in the southwestern United States. It rarely forms root “knees,” and Mexican highland trees can develop exceptionally stout trunks.

A deciduous conifer native to the southeastern United States, baldcypress is notable for lacy needles that turn russet-red in autumn. Its trunk is often surrounded by woody root projections called cypress knees.

A herbaceous perennial native to woodlands and rocky areas of eastern North America, it bears nodding flowers with red nectar-bearing spurs and yellow petals. Children in parts of the United States traditionally bit off the spur ends for their sweet nectar.
edibilityNote: Children in Illinois, Massachusetts and Wisconsin traditionally bit off the flower-spur ends for the sweet nectar.

summary: A short-lived deciduous tree native to northern North America. Older trees have thin white bark that peels in paper-like layers, while younger bark is reddish-brown. Its sap is boiled down to make birch syrup, though production is currently small-scale in Alaska and Yukon.
edibilityNote: The sap is boiled down into birch syrup, currently produced by a few small-scale operations in Alaska and Yukon.

summary: A deciduous tree native to eastern North America. It often has several stems and smooth greyish-white bark with black triangular patches beneath the branches; unlike paper birch, its bark does not peel readily.

A herbaceous perennial native to the eastern United States and extending west to Texas and Kansas, narrow-leaved blue-eyed grass grows from underground stems. Its six blue flower parts have pointed tips and darken toward a yellow centre.

A perennial flowering plant native to California and Oregon in and west of the Sierra Nevada, with its range extending into Baja California. Its flowers are usually blue to purple, but occasional plants have white flowers. After flowering, it dies back to the ground and remains dormant through summer.

An annual herb native to California's Mojave and Sonoran deserts. Its bright blue flowers may be bell-shaped, funnel-shaped or flattened, sometimes with white throat spots; its juice, sap or hairs may irritate skin.

An evergreen, tree-like palm native to the far southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico. Its waxy fan-shaped leaves have long white threads between their segments, and its sweet fruit pulp is eaten raw, cooked or ground into flour; the bud is also eaten.
edibilityNote: Sweet fruit pulp was eaten raw, cooked or as flour by Native Americans; the bud, or heart of palm, is also eaten.

summary: A widely branched tree endemic to New Zealand, the cabbage tree has a stout, straight trunk crowned by dense clusters of sword-shaped leaves. In spring and early summer, it produces large sprays of sweetly scented flowers.
edibilityNote: Māori ate raw or cooked leaf hearts and steam-cooked dried stems and fleshy rhizomes as a sweet, carbohydrate-rich food.

summary: An annual herb of uncertain origin, thought to be native to Asia and North America. It bears white or yellow flower heads and commonly grows in fields, forests and disturbed places. It can be used as a potherb.
edibilityNote: Used as a potherb.

summary: An annual flowering herb native to tropical America and widely naturalized in warm regions worldwide. Its rough black fruits carry barbed tips that catch on animals, people and clothing. The resin-flavoured leaves are eaten raw, cooked in stews or dried for storage.
edibilityNote: The resin-flavoured leaves are eaten raw, in stews or dried for storage; soldiers also used the herb as a vegetable during the Vietnam War.

summary: A flowering vine native to eastern and central North America, extending south to eastern Mexico and Guatemala. Its tendrils end in adhesive pads, and its usually five-part leaves may turn bright red in autumn. Its berries contain toxic oxalic acid and can cause kidney damage or death in humans.
edibilityNote: Berries contain toxic oxalic acid and have caused kidney damage and death in humans.

summary: A perennial herb native across much of the Northern Hemisphere, woodland strawberry produces strongly flavoured edible fruit and usually spreads by runners. It has toothed leaves arranged in threes and soft, hairy white flowers held above the foliage.
edibilityNote: The fruit has been eaten since the Stone Age and is collected or cultivated for domestic use, preserves, sauces and liqueurs.

summary: A perennial shrub native to the tropical Americas, common lantana can form dense thickets. Its crushed leaves have a strong odour, while its clustered flowers occur in many colours and typically change colour after pollination.
edibilityNote: Human toxicity is undetermined: unripe green fruits are reported toxic, while some studies describe ripe fruit as edible.

summary: Bushy perennial herb native to dry tropical regions of Mexico, Guatemala, Chile and Peru. Its strongly fragrant flowers open from late afternoon or dusk until morning, and differently coloured or patterned blooms can appear together on one plant.
edibilityNote: Cooked leaves are eaten only as emergency food; flowers provide edible colouring for cakes and jellies. Seeds are considered poisonous.

summary: A deciduous shrub or small tree native to North America, with leaves divided into three leaflets dotted with oil glands. The foliage turns rusty yellow in autumn, and small greenish-white flowers grow in clusters at branch tips.

Biennial herb native to North American plains, foothills and high-elevation conifer forests, with some varieties restricted to California. Its upright stems rise from a basal rosette and carry dense clusters of four-petalled flowers, usually golden, yellow or tangerine but sometimes red, white or purple. In Zuni tradition, the flowers and fruit are eaten as an emetic for stomach aches.
edibilityNote: In Zuni tradition, the flowers and fruit are eaten as an emetic for stomach aches.

summary: Annual herb native to California, Baja California and Oregon. Its flowers vary from blue with white centres to entirely white, often showing blue veins and black dots; the three varieties differ in colour and regional habitat.

A long-lived terrestrial orchid widespread across much of Europe and Asia and northern Africa, and introduced in North America. It has broad, strongly ribbed dull-green leaves and drooping flower clusters, though rare white plants lacking chlorophyll have also been found.

A perennial flowering plant native to Europe and northern, central and eastern Asia. It has slender blue-green leaves and dense clusters of pale-yellow, snapdragon-like flowers with orange-yellow markings, usually appearing from midsummer to mid-autumn.

A flowering plant native to the western United States and British Columbia, California beeplant has paired, toothed blue-green leaves on slender square stems. Its brownish-magenta flowers strongly attract bees, and it hosts variable checkerspot larvae.
An agave native to Mexico and Central America, it is used to make the distilled alcoholic drink mezcal. The ornamental cultivar 'Marginata' has white-edged leaves.
edibilityNote: Used to make mezcal, a distilled alcoholic beverage.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to California’s Central Valley and the foothills of the Sierra Nevada and Coast Ranges. Its bell-shaped flowers grade from blue-violet tips through purple spots to yellow throats, creating a memorable three-colour pattern.

A bulb-forming perennial native to the northern Bokkeveld Escarpment in South Africa’s west-central Cape Provinces. Its bi- or tri-coloured flowers have a golden centre and a small brown ring surrounded by another colour. It has escaped from gardens and become introduced in California and Australia.

A perennial flowering herb of unstated native origin, field chickweed occurs widely across Europe and North America and in parts of South America. It may form a mat, clump, creeping growth or upright stems, and bears hairy foliage and five deeply lobed white petals.

Annual legume native to southern Europe and the region of Syria. Its contorted, densely hairy pods resemble prickly caterpillars; in some Mediterranean countries, the leaves are used as a salad herb and the pods may be added to salads.
edibilityNote: Leaves are used as a salad herb in some Mediterranean countries; densely hairy pods may be added to salads.

summary: Deciduous tree native to the southeastern United States, though its original range is somewhat uncertain. Its large, heart-shaped leaves unusually secrete nectar around flowering time. It bears showy white, trumpet-shaped flowers marked with yellow and purple, followed by long, thin seed pods that often remain through winter.
An evergreen oak native to southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa, Quercus suber develops thick, deeply cracked bark. This bark supplies cork and can be harvested repeatedly from mature trees.

A parasitic perennial flowering plant of dry, often saline habitats. It lacks chlorophyll and lives mostly underground attached to a host’s roots, producing a fleshy, club-shaped mass of minute dark-red or purplish flowers after winter rain.
edibilityNote: Bedouin people ate cleaned, peeled fresh spikes; it was also a famine food, last reported in the 19th-century Canary Islands.

summary: Flowering tree native to Asia and Australia, the weeping fig has gracefully drooping branches and glossy oval leaves. Its fruit is edible, though the species is not usually grown for fruit.
edibilityNote: The fruit is edible and figs tend to be eaten dried, but the species is not usually grown for its fruit.

summary: A triplet lily native to California and occasionally found in southwestern Oregon, it has a bare stem topped by purple or blue, sharply six-pointed flowers. Its corm is edible and resembles a potato in taste and use.
edibilityNote: The corm is edible and similar to a potato in taste and use.

summary: An aquatic plant found in slow or still waters from Central America to northern Canada, with additional reports from Brazil and Guyana. Its fragrant white flowers open by day, close at night and pull their developing fruit underwater after pollination. Its seeds, flowers and rhizomes can be eaten raw or cooked.
edibilityNote: The seeds, flowers and rhizomes are edible either raw or cooked.

summary: Aquatic flowering plant endemic to the eastern United States, growing in ponds, streams and shallow lakes. Its pointed oval leaves repel water, and the tiny green sheath around its flower spike withers very early.

A thorny shrub or small tree native to Europe. It has deeply lobed leaves and late-spring white or pink flowers, followed by red haws containing a stone-encased seed. The dry-fleshed haws are commonly made into preserves, syrups or wine, while young leaves and petals are also edible.
edibilityNote: Dry-fleshed haws are commonly made into preserves, syrups or wine; young leaves and petals are edible, with petals recorded in a medieval English pottage.

summary: A cactus endemic to a small area of the coastal mountains of south-eastern Brazil, it naturally grows on trees or rocks in moist forests. Its leafless green stems consist of flattened, toothed segments with cut-off ends, and its colourful flowers appear around May in its natural habitat but in October to November under Northern Hemisphere cultivation.
Flowering plant native from southern Siberia to northern and central China. Its wavy-edged leaves, yellow-white to greenish-white flowers and small fruit distinguish it from related rhubarbs.
edibilityNote: It was among three taxa grown as vegetable crops in England and Scandinavia by the early 18th century.

summary: Woody deciduous climbing vine native to wet forests and stream banks of the southeastern United States. It bears dense clusters of blue-purple flowers and numerous bean-like seed pods that are poisonous.
edibilityNote: Bark, branches, pods, roots and seeds contain wisterin; flower toxicity is debated. Eating one or two pods can cause gastrointestinal poisoning.

summary: Flowering plant native to the Mediterranean Basin. It has gland-dotted, hairy foliage and showy purple-and-white hooded flowers, and remains green while drawing nutrients from other plants' roots.

Deciduous, twiggy shrub or small tree indigenous to Saudi Arabia and the Sinai Peninsula. Its fragile woody branchlets fall in autumn with their small, scale-like leaves. Tiny pink flowers form narrow, feather-like spikes, often blooming before the leaves in May and sometimes again in August.
edibilityNote: Its juice is an ingredient in Gaz, a Persian delicacy from Isfahan.

summary: A green seaweed with no explicitly stated native origin, it occurs in shallow waters on both sides of the Atlantic and in the Mediterranean. It forms dense growth on sand and consists of multiple blades linked by runners, yet each plant is one giant cell with many nuclei.
A flowering plant native to Colombia, Passiflora antioquiensis is also known as the red banana passionfruit. It has received the Royal Horticultural Society’s Award of Garden Merit.

A perennial vine native to southern Brazil through Paraguay to northern Argentina, common passionfruit bears either yellow or dark purple fruit. The round to oval fruit has a juicy, seed-filled interior and is eaten fresh or made into juice.
edibilityNote: The sweet, seedy fruit is eaten fresh and juiced, sometimes blended with other fruit juices.

summary: Evergreen vine native to the Amazon from Peru to eastern Brazil. Its four-winged stems bear fragrant flowers with curved red parts and purple-and-white fringes, followed by edible yellow to bright orange passion fruit prized by local people.
edibilityNote: It bears edible passion fruit that is highly prized by local people.

summary: Perennial vine endemic to the Americas and restricted to Andean highlands from Venezuela to Bolivia. Its large pink to red tubular flowers can remain open for three to five days, and its leaves have three lobes.

A deciduous or semi-evergreen vine native to South America, bluecrown passionflower climbs with tendrils and has lobed leaves. Its fragrant blue-and-white flowers have a striking multicoloured fringe, followed by oval orange fruit. The ripe fruit is edible to humans, though its flavour is sometimes described as bland or unpleasant.
edibilityNote: The ripe fruit is edible to humans, but its flavour is sometimes described as bland, undesirable, insipid or unpleasant.

summary: A fast-growing shrub or small tree native to moist areas of Australia’s east coast, from southeastern Queensland to eastern Victoria. Its evergreen leaves have wavy edges, and conspicuous orange woody fruits remain for several months after spring or early-summer flowering.

A bulb-forming perennial native across much of Europe from Spain to Ukraine, the common snowdrop is among the first bulbs to flower in spring. Each bulb generally produces two narrow grey-green leaves and one nodding, bell-shaped white flower, whose inner segments usually carry a green or yellow-green mark.

A herbaceous perennial native to Europe. It creeps along the ground and roots at stem nodes, with stems hairy only on two opposite sides and deep-blue, four-lobed flowers that wilt quickly when picked.
edibilityNote: Used internally as tea in traditional Austrian medicine; tea-making was also popular in 18th-century Britain.

summary: Annual grass whose native origin is not stated, now widespread worldwide as a common weed. Its flower heads have long, thin, radiating branches that may be reddish or purple. The edible seeds require hand harvesting and were historically cooked in soups and porridges in medieval Eastern Europe.
edibilityNote: Seeds were used as grain, including in medieval Eastern European soups and porridges; harvesting for human consumption must be done by hand.

summary: A hardy perennial native to temperate Europe and northern Asia, growing in damp grasslands, woods, meadows and rocky places. It bears cup-shaped blue or white flowers and is cultivated in borders and rock gardens.
An annual herb native to northern North America. Its heads contain orange florets and usually lack yellow rays; its flat dark fruits bear two hornlike, barbed tips that catch on animals.
An annual herb most likely native to the central United States. It has numerous yellow flower heads, while its dry fruits bear barbs that catch on fur or clothing.

An annual to short-lived perennial flowering plant native to Europe, Turkey, the Caucasus, Siberia, the western Himalayas and northwestern Africa. It has small grey-blue, saucer-shaped flowers with hooked hairs around their bases, followed by dark brown, shiny fruits.

Wildflower endemic to California, Elegant Clarkia has a slender, hairless, waxy red stem and showy pink, red or purple flowers. Its long white pistil and prominent red stamens make it easy to recognize.
edibilityNote: Although not typically eaten, the seeds can be eaten raw or cooked and ground into a fine powder.

summary: Evergreen perennial subshrub native to the Mediterranean region. Its woody stems carry greyish leaves and blue to purple flowers. It has a savory, slightly peppery flavor and a long history as a culinary herb in several European, Middle Eastern, British and American dishes.
edibilityNote: Long-used culinary herb with a savory, slightly peppery flavor, eaten in dishes across several cuisines.

summary: Herbaceous perennial native to Europe and Asia. It spreads aggressively through underground rhizomes and can crowd out other plants. Tender young leaves have been eaten since antiquity as a spring vegetable, often in soup; after flowering they become pungent and may have a laxative effect.
edibilityNote: Tender young leaves have served as a spring vegetable since antiquity, especially in soup; after flowering they taste pungent and may have a laxative effect.

summary: An evergreen shrub native to Western Europe. Its young shoots and leaves form green spines, while coconut-scented yellow flowers appear throughout the year, especially in spring.
edibilityNote: The fragrant petals have culinary uses.

summary: An evergreen perennial native to New Zealand and Norfolk Island, it forms clumps of long, straplike leaves beneath much taller yellow or red flower shoots. Its leaf fibre has long been used in Māori textiles and later for rope and sails.

A short-lived perennial or annual flowering plant native to northern Mexico and the southern and central United States. Its vivid, pinwheel-like flower heads combine red, orange and yellow, usually blooming from May to July but nearly year-round in some areas. It commonly grows on sandy plains, in deserts and beside roads.

A succulent evergreen perennial native to the mountains of southern Europe, houseleek forms grey-green rosettes whose leaves are often tinged rose-red. It spreads by offsets and bears clusters of reddish-purple flowers in summer.

A perennial flowering plant native to Europe and possibly originating in the Balkans, common columbine forms bushy clumps and usually bears nodding blue or purple flowers with nectar spurs. It is poisonous: eating fresh leaves or flowers has caused serious symptoms in people.
edibilityNote: Fresh leaves and flowers have caused poisoning symptoms after ingestion; Kew identifies the species as poisonous.

summary: A creeping evergreen perennial native to Europe, spreading by stems that root along the ground. Its rounded leaves grow in opposite pairs, with cup-shaped yellow flowers in summer, and it favours damp places where it can spread vigorously.

A small deciduous tree or large shrub native to central and southern Europe, common laburnum bears hanging clusters of sweet-scented golden flowers in late spring. Its pods contain black seeds with cytisine that are somewhat poisonous to humans, especially when unripe.
edibilityNote: The black seeds contain cytisine and are somewhat poisonous to humans, especially when unripe.

summary: Evening primrose native to much of western and central North America. Its usually reddish stem carries long, narrow leaves beneath a large cluster of fragrant yellow flowers. The flowers open at dusk, wilt the next morning and turn orange or red.

Perennial herb native to Europe, Middle Asia and Siberia, growing in deeply shaded, moist woods. It bears white summer flowers followed by small burr-like fruits, while its above-ground parts die back in winter and leave an underground stem.

A short-lived perennial herb native to Europe, western Asia and northwestern Africa, it has three-part leaves marked by a pale crescent and dense heads of dark-pink flowers. Its flowers and leaves are edible as garnishes or ground into flour, while the flowers are also used for jelly and herbal teas.
edibilityNote: Flowers and leaves are eaten as garnishes or ground into flour; flowers are also used for jelly and herbal teas.

summary: A perennial herb native to Europe, much of temperate Asia and western North Africa. Most subspecies bear hollow hairs on their leaves and stems that cause a painful sting on contact. Young plants and leaves are eaten cooked; soaking or cooking removes the stinging chemicals.
edibilityNote: Young plants and leaves are cooked and eaten; soaking or cooking removes the sting. Leaves and flowers are also dried for tea.

summary: A creeping annual or perennial flowering plant native to the Caribbean and Central and South America. Its compound leaves rapidly fold and droop when touched or shaken, reopening within minutes; they also close in darkness and reopen in light.
edibilityNote: The plant contains toxic alkaloid mimosine, but no human food use or ingestion outcome is documented.

summary: A South American plant that grows as an annual in temperate climates and a branching perennial shrub in the tropics. Its velvety, heart-shaped leaves accompany drooping yellow flowers, followed by golden berries enclosed in inflated, papery husks.
edibilityNote: Ripe berries are eaten fresh or cooked; husks are inedible, and unripe raw fruit, flowers, leaves and stems may cause poisoning.

summary: A large cottonwood poplar native to North America, the eastern cottonwood has triangular, coarsely toothed leaves on flat stalks that tremble in the slightest breeze. Female catkins release numerous small seeds attached to cotton-like strands in early summer.

Large riparian tree native to the southwestern United States and northern through central Mexico. Its smooth young bark becomes deeply fissured and whitish with age; autumn leaves are usually bright yellow, and its fruit resembles cotton hanging from the branches.

A flowering plant native to North America, American searocket commonly grows on beaches and dunes. It is a short, succulent shrub with thick leaves that vary in their teeth and lobes. It is annual in northern latitudes but may survive as a biennial in warmer climates.
edibilityNote: The leaves are edible, preferably cooked and not eaten in large quantities.

summary: A flowering annual herb native from Central Mexico to Nicaragua, red amaranth bears tall stems topped with dark pink flower clusters. Its seeds have been eaten in North and Central America since at least 4000 BC, prepared as grain, flour, porridge, popped seeds or sweets; the leaves are cooked like spinach.
edibilityNote: Seeds are eaten as grain, flour, porridge, popped seeds or sweets; leaves are cooked like spinach, with use documented since at least 4000 BC.

summary: An annual plant native to the Mediterranean region, with green or purplish, roughly triangular leaves. It is gathered wild for food; in Greece the leaves and cooked tender shoots are eaten, while in Lebanon young shoots are cooked as a side dish.
edibilityNote: Wild-gathered leaves and tender or young shoots are eaten, including cooked preparations in Greece and Lebanon.

summary: A twining plant native to Mexico and Central America. It has heart-shaped leaves, brown-haired stems and trumpet-shaped flowers, usually blue, purple or white.

An upright flowering shrub native to the southern United States, Mexico and Central America. It has leaves divided into four or five pairs of egg-shaped leaflets, while its yellow flowers usually contain seven fertile stamens and four sterile ones.

Plant native to South Africa, the narrow-leaf cotton bush is also common in Australia and New Zealand, where it hosts monarch butterflies. Eating significant quantities of its leaves, stems or fruit may be fatal to humans and livestock.
edibilityNote: Eating significant quantities of the leaves, stems or fruit may be fatal to humans.

summary: A spreading shrub native to Brazil, Bolivia, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, spearleaf swampmallow has hibiscus-like pink flowers with red throats. Its first spring flowers are often much smaller and remain closed, while profuse flowering occurs during summer and autumn.

A lily endemic to Taiwan, it has also become naturalized in scattered parts of Africa, Australia and the Americas. From June to December it bears one to five fragrant, funnel-shaped flowers that are pure white inside and purple outside.

Evergreen conifer endemic to New Zealand, rimu has distinctive drooping foliage with slender, hanging branchlets. Its grey to dark-brown bark flakes away to reveal wavy parallel ridges resembling contour lines on a map.
edibilityNote: Its fruit was a significant seasonal food for Māori; in 1773, James Cook brewed beer from young branch tips.

summary: A coniferous tree native to eastern North America, from Pennsylvania and the Great Lakes region to Manitoba and Newfoundland. It grows tall and straight, with flaky orange-red bark in the upper crown, and older trees may have long branchless trunks beneath the canopy.

A large pine native to eastern North America, eastern white pine has flexible bluish-green needles usually bundled in fives. Mature trees can live for centuries and tower over mixed forests. During winter starvation, Algonquian peoples dried and pounded the inner bark into flour; Ojibwe people also stewed young male cones with meat, and the seeds are sweet and nutritious.
edibilityNote: Historically, inner bark was made into flour during winter starvation; Ojibwe people stewed young male cones, and the seeds are sweet and nutritious.

summary: Annual herb endemic to Morocco. Its violet-purple flowers have two lips, a straight rear spur and a small yellow or white throat spot. It is grown ornamentally, although many cultivated plants are hybrids with related species.

A flowering tree native to Maluku, New Guinea, the Northern Territory and Queensland. It has bright yellow to golden-yellow flower spikes and strongly curved or spirally coiled, leathery to woody pods.
A flowering tree native to Brazil. Its black, dry pods curve like ears and contain several hard, glossy seeds; when crushed, the pods smell sweet and produce sticky material.

A deciduous shrub native to the Caucasus and northeastern Turkey, sweet mock orange has abundant, bowl-shaped white flowers with a strong fragrance. Cultivated varieties may be less fragrant than the species.
edibilityNote: The blossoms are locally made into tea in Latvia and Estonia; the leaves have also been suggested for adding cucumber-like flavour to drinks.

summary: A perennial flowering vine native to Europe and Asia, tufted vetch climbs nearby plants using branched, noose-like tendrils. It produces abundant one-sided clusters of purple to violet pea-shaped flowers and can be distinguished from hairy vetch by its smooth stem.

An erect herbaceous perennial native to the Himalayas of India, Nepal, and Bhutan. Its tall stems carry long bright-green leaves and dense spikes of very fragrant pale-yellow and red flowers in late summer.
A shrub native to China. It has light-brown peeling bark, gracefully arching branches and showy paired pink, bell-shaped flowers in late spring.

A flowering herbaceous perennial native to Europe, Western Asia and North Africa, marsh mallow is covered in soft hairs and bears pale pink or lilac flowers. Its young leaves can be cooked, flower buds pickled, and roots boiled before frying or boiled and sweetened for candy.
edibilityNote: Young leaves are cooked, buds pickled, and roots boiled before frying or sweetened for candy; marsh mallow was historically a Roman delicacy.

summary: An annual or biennial thistle native from the Mediterranean and much of Europe east to Central Asia and India, extending south to Ethiopia. It has red-purple flower heads and shiny green leaves marked with milk-white veins and edged with spines.
edibilityNote: Leaves and stems are boiled with salt after removing spines; roots are eaten raw or roasted, and flower heads cooked like artichokes.

summary: A thorny annual herb native to the Mediterranean Basin, yellow star-thistle begins as a non-spiny leaf rosette before producing stems with yellow, sharply spined flower heads. It commonly occupies disturbed ground and has become invasive in many regions outside its native range.

Aquatic plant native to the Americas, growing along wetland margins from eastern Canada to Argentina. Its slate-blue flowers have yellow markings, and the seed-bearing stem bends to submerge the developing fruits and seeds.
edibilityNote: Young leafstalks are eaten raw after removing unripe fruits, or cooked; seeds are eaten raw or ground into grain.

summary: Submerged marine flowering plant native to northern-latitude coastlines of North America and Eurasia. Its hairlike leaves grow from rhizomes that can spread into seabed meadows; one cloned meadow was genetically estimated at 3,000 years old. The Seri people of Mexico eat the grains toasted and ground into paste, while a Spanish chef has cultivated them in Cádiz as “sea rice.”
edibilityNote: The Seri toast and grind the grains into paste; a Spanish chef has cultivated and harvested them as “sea rice” in Cádiz.
