summary: A perennial flowering plant native to western Europe, from Spain and Portugal east to Germany and north to England and Wales. It grows from a bulb and bears pale yellow flowers with a darker central trumpet. Its bulbs and leaves contain the poison lycorine and should never be eaten.
edibilityNote: Bulbs and leaves contain lycorine and should never be eaten.

summary: Annual flowering herb native to Eurasia. Its square stems carry leaves that shade from green below to purple above, and unlike true nettles it cannot sting. Young tops and leaves are eaten in salads, stir-fries or sauces, while flowers can be crystallized with sugar and egg white.
edibilityNote: Young tops and leaves are used in salads, stir-fries or sauces; flowers can be crystallized with sugar and egg white.

summary: Flowering perennial native to the Caucasus. It has large, heart-shaped leaves, usually marked white or cream, and sprays of small blue flowers from mid-spring.

An annual herb probably native to Central America, jimsonweed has night-opening trumpet-shaped flowers and egg-shaped seed capsules that may be spiny. It is poisonous: all parts contain dangerous tropane alkaloids, and ingestion can cause delirium, hallucinations and potentially fatal poisoning.
edibilityNote: All parts contain dangerous tropane alkaloids; ingestion can cause severe poisoning and carries a high risk of fatal overdose.

summary: A tuberous perennial herb native around the Black Sea and in a separate Mediterranean population from Turkey’s Hatay Province through Lebanon to northern Israel. Its rounded or heart-shaped leaves vary from green to silver-patterned, and its squat pink, magenta or white flowers bloom from winter into spring.

A perennial flowering plant native to Bulgaria, Hungary, Albania and the former Yugoslavia. Among the first crocuses to bloom, it bears slender flowers ranging from pale silvery lilac to reddish purple, although one variant is white.

A perennial flowering herb native across Europe and Asia, white deadnettle generally grows in moist, fertile ground. Its softly hairy, nettle-like leaves do not sting, and it bears white flowers around the upper stem.
edibilityNote: Young shoots and leaves can be cooked as a vegetable.

summary: An evergreen climbing shrub native and endemic to Madeira, Madeiran ivy commonly grows on rocky slopes, soil and tree trunks, especially in laurel forest. Its aerial roots cling to trees, cliffs and walls, while its stems may be tinged red or purple and its round fruits turn black when ripe.

A clinging evergreen vine native to most of Europe and parts of western Asia, it climbs with strongly gripping aerial rootlets or spreads as groundcover. Creeping stems carry lobed leaves, while flowering stems have unlobed heart-shaped leaves; its berries are somewhat poisonous to humans.
edibilityNote: The berries are somewhat poisonous to humans.

summary: A variable climbing wild rose native to Europe, northwest Africa and western Asia, it has arching stems armed with hooked prickles. Its sweet-scented summer flowers range from white to deep pink and mature into red-orange hips in autumn.
edibilityNote: Ripe autumn hips are eaten after avoiding their internal hairs or made into drinks and preserves; flowers and petals are also eaten.

summary: A vigorous deciduous twining climber native to much of Europe, North Africa, Turkey and the Caucasus, it bears showy clusters of creamy white or yellowish tubular flowers. The flowers may be flushed pink or red and are far more strongly scented at night than during the day.

Annual honesty is an annual or biennial flowering plant native to southern Europe, from Spain to Romania. Its white, pink or violet flowers are followed by translucent, disc-shaped fruits whose silvery central membranes may persist through winter and are often used in dried arrangements.

A perennial herb native to temperate Eurasia, wood avens grows along shady woodland edges and hedgerows. Its fresh root smells like cloves, while its hairy fruits bear hooked burrs that catch on animal fur.
edibilityNote: Leaves can be cooked like spinach; roots are used to spice soups and flavour ale.

summary: A deciduous perennial herb native to Europe and southwestern Asia. It has apricot-scented flower spikes, while its soft hairs and hooked fruits readily cling to animals and clothing.
A flowering plant native to most temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere, it has yellow flowers and pointed leaves with toothed, sometimes nearly hooked margins.

A spiny shrub native to Europe, it is especially common across much of the British Isles. Its broad, toothed leaflets grow in groups of three or five, and pink or magenta flowers produce nearly black fruit.
Annual poppy native to Europe, North Africa and southwestern Asia. It has showy pale-red flowers, elongated hairless seed capsules and white to yellowish latex released from damaged tissue.

A small, usually biennial herb considered native in North America, it also occurs widely across Europe and North Africa. Bruised or uprooted plants have a strong unpleasant smell, while ripe fruits are explosively ejected from the plant.

Perennial plant with no native origin specified, common across much of Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Turkmenistan. It flowers in summer and bears toxic fruit that has been used in traditional medicine.
edibilityNote: The fruit is toxic.

summary: A deciduous shrub native to Europe, northern Africa and central Asia. Its early-summer flower clusters have a ring of large, sterile white flowers around smaller fertile ones, followed by bright red, single-seeded fruits.
edibilityNote: Fruit is edible only in small quantities and can be made into jelly; large amounts are mildly toxic and may cause vomiting or diarrhoea.

summary: A robust herbaceous perennial native to Europe and Asia, including China, Japan, Kazakhstan, the Koreas, Mongolia, Siberia, Russia and Turkmenistan. It has aromatic, dark-green, deeply toothed leaves and small golden-yellow flowers in dense, flat-topped clusters in summer.
edibilityNote: Used to add aroma and bitterness to vermouth and in sweet and savoury dishes.

summary: A tall deciduous shrub native to Europe, northernmost Africa and western Asia. Unlike other buckthorns, it has no thorns; cut bark reveals a bright lemon-yellow inner layer, and its berries ripen from green through red to black.

A robust perennial herb native to Europe, northwestern Africa, parts of western and central Asia, and the Caucasus. It has reddish hairy stems, deeply lobed leaves and fluffy mauve flower heads that attract many insects.

A herbaceous perennial native to Europe and southwestern Asia, musk mallow has hairy stems and leaves that become deeply divided higher on the plant. Its five-petalled pink flowers bloom in summer and have a distinctive musky scent.
edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers can be added to salads, and seeds are described as edible, although the passage flags a citation as needed.

summary: An annual flowering herb native to Europe and northwestern Asia. It has square, hairy stems with swollen joints and small, snapdragon-like flowers patterned in purple, pink or white; it readily occupies disturbed ground and roadsides.

An annual or perennial flowering herb native to Europe and southwestern Asia. It has erect hairy stems with milky sap, toothed leaves, and loose clusters of pale yellow flowers. Its young leaves are edible in salads or cooked like spinach, though their fine hairs may make them preferable mixed with other vegetables.
edibilityNote: Young leaves can be eaten in salads or cooked like spinach; their fine hairs may make mixing with other vegetables preferable.

summary: A biennial flowering herb, rarely a short-lived perennial, native to Eurasia and North Africa. Its prickly stems and leaves carry lavender flower heads that open in bands and dry into persistent cones of hard, spine-tipped bracts.

Rhizomatous flowering perennial native to southern Africa. It has broad, arrow-shaped leaves and a large white sheath surrounding a fragrant yellow flower spike. Eating the raw plant may severely burn and swell the mouth and throat and cause stomach pain and diarrhoea.
edibilityNote: The raw plant contains calcium oxalate and may cause severe mouth and throat irritation, stomach pain and diarrhoea.

summary: Shrub or tree native to southeastern Europe and Turkey. Its branching twigs carry tiny linear leaves and dense flower spikes, with each small flower bearing four pink petals. Introduced populations are invasive in parts of western North America and elsewhere.
A flowering tree or shrub native to China and Korea. It tolerates moist, salty soils and has tiny scale-like leaves and dense clusters of fragrant flowers, usually pink but ranging from white to red.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native to Europe and Asia, it has arching reddish stems and pale-green, feathery foliage. Upright plumes of small pink flowers cover new growth from late summer to early autumn.

A shrub or small tree endemic to the Canary Islands, it is believed to occur on every island except El Hierro. It is common at lower elevations, including shores and estuaries, and tolerates some salinity.

An evergreen flowering tree native across parts of Africa, the Middle East, and western and southern Asia, athel tamarisk grows along watercourses in arid areas. Its tiny leaves exude salt that forms a crystalline crust, while nectar from its blossoms produces distinctively flavoured honey.
edibilityNote: Nectar from the blossoms produces high-quality honey described as having a unique taste.

summary: A shrub native to and endemic to the western Mediterranean region. It bears pink or white flowers in dense spikes and tolerates salty conditions, commonly forming thickets beside seasonal rivers and ravines in dry areas.
Herbaceous perennial native to Southern Europe. Its scalloped leaves hold beads of water in wet weather, while dense clusters of chartreuse-yellow flowers rise above the foliage.

Annual or perennial herb native to southern Africa, including Lesotho and several South African provinces. It forms spreading rosettes and runners, with deeply divided leaves densely covered in white woolly hairs underneath. Its daisy-like flowers have yellow centers and white or yellow outer petals, but the plant can become invasive where introduced.

Edible succulent plant probably native to southern Africa. Its long ground-hugging stems root at their joints to form carpets, with fleshy pointed leaves and deep-magenta flowers. Leaves may be eaten raw, cooked or pickled; fruit should be fully ripe and may be laxative in large quantities.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw, cooked or pickled; fully ripe fruit is edible but has little flesh and may be laxative in quantity.

summary: Bulb-growing perennial ornamental native to the Mediterranean region from Portugal to Turkey. It bears clusters of as many as eight white flowers with yellow centres and contains a fragrant compound that humans can scarcely detect but honeybees readily sense.

A corm-growing perennial herb endemic to South Africa's Cape Province, it grows in winter, flowers in spring and rests during summer. Its tall spikes carry neat rows of bright orange-red or scarlet flowers with yellow to orange lower parts.
A perennial maidenhair fern native to California and Baja California. Its trailing leaves have many rounded, lobed green segments, with spore-bearing patches underneath.

A deciduous broadleaf tree native to western North America, red alder is among the world’s largest alders. Its leaf edges curl under, unlike those of other alders, and the leaves darken and wither rather than turning yellow before falling.

A flowering plant native to South Africa's Cape Province, the red hot poker has lily-like leaves and tall flowerheads of red, orange and yellow. Its many varieties bloom at different times during the growing season.

A perennial herb native to Europe and temperate Asia, oxeye daisy spreads through seeds and shallow creeping underground stems. Its flower heads have white rays around yellow centres, and its unopened buds can be marinated like capers.
edibilityNote: Unopened flower buds can be marinated and used like capers.

summary: A biennial flowering plant native to Europe, western and central Asia, and north-western Africa, garlic mustard forms low leaf clusters in its first year and flowers the following spring. Its crushed leaves smell of garlic, while its small white flowers are cross-shaped and grow in dense clusters.
edibilityNote: Chopped leaves, especially young ones, flavour salads and sauces; flowers and fruit are sometimes included. Young first-year plants contain cyanide, whose gas is eliminated by chopping.

summary: A deciduous tree or shrub considered under a recent definition to be native to most of Europe, parts of Asia and northern Africa. It has paired leaflets and clusters of creamy-white flowers followed by red fruit; the bitter raw fruit is commonly debittered by freezing, cooking or drying before being made into preserves, drinks and other foods.
edibilityNote: Bitter raw fruit is usually frozen, cooked or dried, then made into preserves, juice, alcoholic drinks, tea, flour or savoury accompaniments.

summary: Herbaceous perennial native to Eurasia, meadow buttercup has glossy yellow flowers on ungrooved stems and finely cut, hairy leaflets. Its flower buds begin developing in late summer before the flowering year, and it overwinters as a rosette. The Cherokee cook its leaves and eat them as greens.
edibilityNote: The Cherokee cook the leaves and eat them as greens.

summary: A flowering perennial native to much of Europe and parts of Asia, sweet woodruff has foliage whose sweet scent strengthens as it wilts and persists when dried. It was, and to some extent remains, used to flavour drinks, preserves, ice cream, tea and other foods.
edibilityNote: Historically and partly still used to flavour alcoholic and soft drinks, jelly, jam, ice cream, herbal tea and other sweets.

summary: Perennial herb native to much of Europe, western and central Asia, and parts of Africa and China. Its yellow flowers bear black glands, while translucent leaf glands make the leaves look perforated; each plant can produce thousands of seeds.

A deciduous hardwood tree native to the eastern United States, though its exact native range is uncertain, black locust has deeply furrowed bark and paired prickles that vary greatly between trees. It spreads through root suckers, sometimes forming dense colonies.
edibilityNote: In parts of Europe and Japan, flowers are fried or made into jam; reports call shelled seeds and young pods edible, though bark and leaves are toxic.

summary: A fast-growing mulberry tree native to China and India, white mulberry is widely cultivated for leaves that feed silkworms. Its pollen is released at about half the speed of sound, while its fruit ranges from white or pink in cultivated plants to deep purple in the wild.
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten fresh or dried and made into syrups, wines, spirits, paste or tea; leaves are prepared as tea in Korea.

summary: Sprawling perennial herb native to Europe. Surface runners form dense mats of purple-tinged leaves, while spring stalks carry many blue or purple flowers.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw, in salads or as tea; only small amounts are advised, and older leaves become more bitter.

summary: A moss widespread across temperate regions worldwide, grey-cushioned Grimmia forms small grey-green to orange-yellow cushions, sometimes with silvery leaf tips. Its capsules bend back into the leaves when dry and stand out when moist, and it grows on rocks, concrete and tree trunks.

A small annual or biennial flowering plant native to Eurasia, shepherd’s-purse has heart-shaped seed pods and mucilaginous seeds that trap nematodes. The plant can be eaten raw, with young leaves preferred, and it is cultivated as a leaf vegetable in Asia.
edibilityNote: The plant is eaten raw or cooked; young leaves are preferred, and it is cultivated as a leaf vegetable in Asia.

summary: A biennial herb native to Eurasia and North Africa. It forms shiny dark-green basal rosettes and dense clusters of bright yellow spring flowers, usually with a peppery taste. Young leaves are eaten raw or cooked, buds and flowers are edible, and flower shoots are eaten after cooking.
edibilityNote: Young leaves are eaten raw or cooked; buds and flowers are edible, while flower shoots require cooking.

summary: An annual flowering herb native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa, it has trailing or climbing, hairy stems. Its shallowly lobed leaves resemble ivy, and solitary pale lilac or blue flowers grow from the leaf axils.
A bulbous perennial native to western Atlantic Europe, the bluebell bears sweet-scented violet-blue flowers in nodding, one-sided clusters in spring. It can carpet the floor of ancient woodlands.
edibilityNote: Bluebells, particularly their bulbs, are normally considered toxic.

summary: A large deciduous tree native to Europe and western Asia. It can live for centuries and has deeply fissured bark, while its acorns grow in clusters on long stalks. Though bitter and high in tannins, roasted and ground acorns can serve as a coffee substitute.
edibilityNote: The bitter, tannin-rich acorns can be roasted and ground as a coffee substitute.

summary: Bulbous perennial native to central and southeastern Europe. Its tightly packed, nearly round flowers resemble grape clusters; lower fertile flowers point downward, while paler sterile ones point upward.

Perennial flowering plant native to Eurasia. Its delicately scented flowers appear singly in early spring and are typically pale yellow, although wild white and pink forms occur. The flowers open flat, while the leaves often form a heavily wrinkled, evergreen rosette in favourable habitats.
edibilityNote: Flowers and leaves are edible; leaves may be cooked in soup or used for tea, while young flowers can make wine.

summary: A bulbous perennial native to southern and central Europe and north-western Africa. Its white, star-shaped flowers open late in the day and show a green outer stripe when closed; it can spread aggressively through bulb offsets.
edibilityNote: Historically, some regional cuisines used dried and ground or boiled bulbs, and baked flowers into bread; medical authorities advise against eating any part.

summary: A bulb-forming perennial native to Eurasia, growing in moist woodland. It has broad, pointed leaves and flower stems that are triangular in cross-section; in the British Isles it flowers from April to June.
edibilityNote: All parts are documented as edible; leaves are eaten raw or boiled. Poisonous lookalikes cause mistaken-identity poisonings.

summary: Perennial flowering rush considered native across much of Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas. It forms large clumps of smooth, pith-filled cylindrical stems, with yellowish flower clusters that appear to emerge from the stem's side.
edibilityNote: Reported as an ingredient of hui sup tea, although the source marks this claim as needing a citation.

summary: A perennial native throughout Europe and into western Siberia, common soapwort has sweet-scented pink or sometimes white flowers that open in the evening and smell stronger at night. Boiled leaves or roots produce a lathery cleaning liquid. Despite toxic potential, it is used commercially in tahini and brewing, while the root is often added when making halva in the Middle East.
edibilityNote: Despite toxic potential, it is used commercially in tahini and brewing; in the Middle East, the root is often added while making halva.

summary: A moss native to Eurasia and North America. It is rare in Iceland, where it is known from only two locations and locally listed as vulnerable.
A perennial herb native to Europe, the Mediterranean region and eastward to central Asia. It has a strong smell resembling mould or damp soil and clusters of hairy reddish-purple flowers.
edibilityNote: Syrup can be made from the fresh plant; no purpose or preparation details are given.

summary: A flowering perennial native to Europe and parts of Asia, common valerian bears sweet-smelling white or pink flowers in summer. Its creeping rhizomes have an unpleasant smell.
edibilityNote: It can be consumed as tea.

summary: Herbaceous perennial native to Western Europe, North Africa and Asia. It has showy mauve-purple flowers with dark veins and commonly grows in meadows, hedgerows and fallow fields. Young leaves and shoots are eaten raw or cooked and have a long history as wild food.
edibilityNote: Young leaves and shoots are eaten raw or cooked; boiled young leaves were used as a vegetable in parts of 19th-century Europe.

summary: Perennial herb native to Europe. It has upright stems, toothed lobed leaves and delicate spikes of two-lipped mauve flowers, and has a long history as a medicinal plant.

An annual herb native to Europe and Asia, it often has a brown or black spot at the centre of each leaf. Dense spikes carry tiny pink flowers, followed by shiny black, three-edged fruits. Young leaves may be eaten as a leaf vegetable.
edibilityNote: Young leaves may be eaten as a leaf vegetable.

summary: Annual flowering herb apparently native to central Mexico. Its heavily branched stems produce side shoots at nearly every node, while its stems, leaves and flower bracts range from sparsely to densely hairy. Numerous small flower heads have yellow centres and widely spaced white rays.
edibilityNote: It can be eaten as a pot herb or in salads, though culinary use outside its native range is uncommon except in China.

summary: A flowering plant native to most of Europe and western and central Asia. Its rough, hairy foliage and red-flecked stems accompany flowers that change from pink to vivid blue; when eaten, the plant is toxic to horses and cattle.

Annual climbing herb native to Europe and western Asia. Its leaves end in supporting tendrils, while its short-lived whitish or pale-blue flowers produce small, often densely hairy pods, usually containing two seeds.

A deciduous tree native to much of continental Europe, Britain, southwest Asia and the Atlas Mountains of North Africa. It has five blunt, rounded leaf lobes and paired winged fruits that spread in opposite directions.

A shrub native to China, Korea and Japan, Japanese aucuba grows naturally in moist, shaded forest habitats. Often grown in variegated form, it has clusters of small purplish-brown flowers and red fruit.

Perennial herb native to wetlands in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. Its bright, petal-like sepals are usually yellow, while its floating seeds can be splashed from the fruits by raindrops.
edibilityNote: Early spring greens and buds are eaten cooked but are poisonous raw; very young flower buds have also been prepared like capers.

summary: A fragrant herbaceous perennial native across most of Europe. It forms ground-level leaf rosettes and large yellow flower heads, but is toxic when taken internally.
edibilityNote: It should not be taken orally; eating large amounts, or using small amounts of concentrated arnica, can cause poisoning.

summary: A biennial herb native to Europe and parts of western Asia and northern Africa, common centaury grows in fields and roadsides. It forms a small basal rosette, then an upright leafy stem bearing many flat, pinkish-lavender flowers with yellow anthers.

An annual herb native to most of Europe, northern Africa and much of Asia, it grows on cultivated or disturbed ground. Its single upright stem branches near the top and bears small yellow-green flowers from mid-spring to late summer. The raw plant is poisonous and may cause nausea, vomiting, allergic reactions or skin irritation.
edibilityNote: The raw plant is poisonous and may cause nausea, vomiting, allergic reactions and skin irritation.

summary: A low, spreading evergreen shrub native to mountainous central, eastern and southern Europe. Its dark reddish-pink, slender bell-shaped flowers appear from late winter to early spring, sometimes while the plant is still covered by snow.

A small evergreen shrub native to boreal forest and Arctic tundra throughout the Northern Hemisphere. It spreads into dense colonies and bears edible red berries that are initially bitter, later sweetening on the branch; they are widely eaten raw, cooked, sweetened or preserved.
edibilityNote: The berries are eaten raw or prepared as jams, sauces, drinks, baked goods and other dishes.

summary: A flowering plant native to the mountains of central and south-central Europe, with possible populations in Russia's Republic of Karelia.

A large liverwort with a worldwide distribution, common liverwort usually grows on shaded, moist soil and rocks. It forms flattened, fork-branched rosettes and has separate male and female plants with distinctive disc-like or star-rayed reproductive structures. It is frequently among the first vegetation to appear after a large wildfire.

A liverwort of unstated native origin. It forms rounded, yellow-green rosettes with perforated upper surfaces and usually grows on moist, exposed mud near lakes, ponds and reservoirs or in other damp disturbed ground.

An aquatic floating liverwort whose native origin is not stated. It forms thick mats on and beneath pond surfaces, provides a retreat for young aquarium fish, and can be attached to submerged logs or rocks.

A liverwort species with a cosmopolitan distribution, greasewort grows in damp places ranging from open ground to partial shade. Its thick, fleshy, ribbon-like body is dark green when wet and nearly black when dry; it readily colonizes bare ground but is easily displaced by competing plants.

summary: A liverwort described in the source as native to damp forests in southeastern Asia. It is grown in freshwater aquariums, where its submerged growth resembles miniature coral.

A liverwort species recorded in Europe, Asia and both North and South America, Comb Liverwort inhabits damp ground, springs, bogs and wet rocks. Its creeping or rising body branches regularly into a dense, comb-like form and ranges from green to brown, becoming black when dry.

summary: Extraordinarily tiny leafy liverwort that tolerates drying and is often overlooked. It favours bright, dry places with acidic, lime-poor soil, while its variable but consistently present underleaves help distinguish it from related species.

A liverwort with a subboreal distribution, it is reported across Europe, Macaronesia, northern Africa, Asia and North America. Its rounded, square-to-rectangular leaves form green to nearly black-green mats, often in wet, shaded places such as forest streams, springs, bogs and swamps.

An evergreen shrub endemic to Oregon and California in the United States, blueblossom has glossy green leaves and spring clusters of tiny flowers ranging from shades of blue to nearly white. It attracts birds, butterflies and other pollinators, while honeybees often visit for pollen.

A perennial flowering herb of unstated native origin, naturalized in parts of Western Australia. Its distinctive square stem bears evenly arranged, hairless green leaves that shimmer in direct sunlight, along with pink-purple flowers.

An annual flowering plant native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa. It sprawls across the ground, with fresh green leaves and small flowers that are usually white to pale blue, sometimes lilac; its fruit has two parallel lobes.

A wild carrot occurring in both North and South America. It bears clusters of white or pinkish flowers, and its small taproots are edible carrots. It should not be confused with highly poisonous poison hemlock.
edibilityNote: The small taproots are edible carrots.

summary: A bulb-forming herbaceous perennial endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. Its hanging purple flowers sometimes have a green stripe along the centre of each petal-like segment, and its populations are scattered and usually small.

An edible flowering plant native to Eurasia. Its long fruits have an elongated beak lined with comb-like bristles. In Europe it has long been eaten as a leaf and salad vegetable, both cultivated and gathered wild.
edibilityNote: Long used in Europe as a leaf and salad vegetable; formerly cultivated and also gathered wild.

summary: An annual herb native to parts of Europe and introduced elsewhere, including North America. It has rough, branching stems, unequal white petals tinged pink or red, and greenish or pinkish fruits covered with straight or curved prickles.

A fan palm endemic to Guadalupe Island, Mexico. Its native trees occupy a small grove on the island’s steep northern end, where the maritime climate and terrain produce a rare North American fog oasis.

Annual or biennial flowering plant native across parts of Europe, northern Africa and western Asia. It bears bright-purple flower heads guarded by tough, sharp yellow spines. In western Crete a local variety's leaves are eaten boiled, while southern Italian Arbëreshë communities boil and fry young whorls with other wild greens.
edibilityNote: In western Crete, local leaves are boiled; southern Italian Arbëreshë communities boil and fry young whorls with other wild greens.

summary: Annual, biennial or perennial herb native to western and southern Europe. It grows upright with many branches ending in dandelion-like flower heads, and occurs on hillsides and in sandy clearings.

A small creeping aquatic perennial native to North Africa, Europe, the Caucasus and parts of the Levant. It grows in wetlands, marshes and swamps, producing shiny, rounded leaves with umbrella-like veins.
edibilityNote: Described as edible, with a slight carrot smell, but the source flags this claim as needing citation.

summary: A rootless parasitic plant native from Macaronesia across most of Europe to northwestern China, and also present in western North Africa, clover dodder has thread-like pink, red, yellow or purple stems. It coils around many kinds of host plant and draws water and nutrients from them.

A bulb-growing herbaceous perennial native to Europe and western Russia, south through Turkey to Syria. It usually has two shiny, fleshy leaves and bears upward-facing violet-blue spring flowers, which are occasionally white, pink or purple.

Herbaceous plant native to the Mediterranean region across Eurasia, North Africa and Western Asia. It has notably long, stiff, awl-shaped leaves and has become naturalized in western North America, South America, Hawaii and Australia.

Clumping perennial herb native to South Africa. It usually has slender linear leaves with dull green upper surfaces and white woolly undersides, plus solitary bright-yellow flower heads that close at night; the rare variety ovalis instead has more oval leaves and is restricted near Grahamstown.

A vernal-pool plant with no stated native origin, it is found mainly in California and extends into Oregon and northern Baja California. Its tiny flower heads resemble white cotton balls, giving individual plants the informal name Q-tips.

Low-growing annual, rarely a short-lived perennial, native to the Mediterranean Basin and Macaronesia. It bears dense clusters of small, honey-scented flowers, and its petals, leaves and tender stems can be eaten raw or cooked.
edibilityNote: Petals, leaves and tender stems can be eaten raw or cooked.

summary: A flowering plant native to the western Mediterranean Basin in Europe and northern Africa. Its slender, much-branched stems bear narrow-lobed upper leaves and small yellow flowers; after maturity, the dead plant uproots and tumbles in the wind, spreading seed.
edibilityNote: The spicy leaves can be used to make wasabi or mixed into salads and other dishes.

summary: A petite annual herb native to Europe, it also occurs as an introduced plant in places including parts of North America. It grows in disturbed sites such as pavement cracks and bears solitary flowers that usually have four sepals and no petals.

Small annual herb native to several parts of North America and found in many habitats. Its threadlike green or purplish stems may stand upright or trail, and each slender flower stalk carries one flower, usually with five tiny white petals.

An annual plant native to Europe, Macaronesia, Siberia, northwestern India, northwestern Africa and the highlands of eastern tropical Africa. Its tiny flowers have five white petals, and seeds buried in soil can survive for several years.

Annual or perennial spikesedge widespread across Europe, central and southeastern Asia, the Americas, and probably introduced in Australia. Its creeping underground stem produces short, grasslike stems and tiny pointed flower spikes in marshes, seasonal pools, and bogs.

summary: A herbaceous perennial native to Europe, western Asia and northwest Africa. Pale spore-bearing stems emerge in early spring before the green, heavily branched sterile stems, which last from late spring to autumn.

Annual plant native to most of Europe, northern Africa and western Asia, typically occurring on cultivated or disturbed ground. It has smooth stems, green flowers and kidney-shaped glands with long, thin horns. Its whole plant, including the root, was formerly eaten as Polish famine food after boiling in milk.
edibilityNote: In Poland, the whole plant, including its root, was formerly eaten as famine food after being boiled in milk.

summary: A perennial shrub or small tree native to southeastern Australia, it has rigid, prickly leaf-like structures crowded in whorled bundles. From July to December it produces densely packed pale-yellow flower spikes, followed by narrow, flattened seed pods.

An evergreen shrub native to South Australia, Victoria and Tasmania. It produces short clusters of yellow flowers periodically throughout the year. Indigenous Australians ate its gum after softening it in water to relieve chest pains.
edibilityNote: Indigenous Australians ate the gum after softening it in water, historically to relieve chest pains.

summary: An annual or short-lived perennial native to Africa and Eurasia, black medick bears tight bunches of small yellow flowers. Its single-seeded pods harden and turn black when ripe.

Perennial legume that appears to have originated in south-central Asia. It has a deep root system and usually lives four to eight years, though some varieties in suitable climates can exceed 20 years; it is widely used as ruminant feed in temperate, dry regions.

A yellow-flowered annual herb native from Macaronesia and northern Africa through Europe to temperate and tropical Asia. Its three-part leaves release a sweet, cloying scent when crushed, and the plant can maintain strong germination and growth in salty soils.

An annual or biennial legume native to Eurasia and introduced to North America, Africa and Australia. It has three-part leaves, yellow spring-to-summer flowers and a characteristic sweet odor; its seeds can remain viable for up to 30 years.

Flowering annual herb native to Europe and western Asia. Its leaves have three leaflets, while its distinctive yellow flower heads resemble hops. The flowers turn brown as they age and dry, enclosing a single-seeded pod.

Hairy annual flowering herb native to Eurasia and North Africa. Its erect stems carry three-part leaves and pink flower clusters with fine-haired cups whose needle-like lobes may harden into bristles as the plant ages.

Annual flowering herb native to much of Eurasia, the Mediterranean region and North Africa. It begins as a flat rosette of deeply lobed leaves on red stalks, then bears purple-streaked lavender flowers and long-beaked fruit.
A weedy annual or biennial herb native to much of Eurasia and North Africa. It smells musky when bruised, and its long-beaked fruits open to reveal feathery, wind-dispersed seeds.
edibilityNote: The species is described as edible, but no plant part or preparation is specified.

summary: An annual grasslike rush with a native range described as circumpolar across tropical to subarctic areas of both hemispheres. It forms green clumps of thin stems with a few threadlike leaves and grows in moist, muddy places.

A perennial rush found in creek beds and freshwater marshes of the Southwestern United States. It has flat, tapering leaves and small green flowers that usually remain enclosed in reddish-tipped bracts. Its shoots can take up and store selenate, so the plant is used for phytoremediation.

This flowering mint is native to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, though its native range is thought to centre on the eastern Mediterranean. Crushed leaves smell strongly of spearmint, and small mauve flowers form dense, widely spaced whorls along the stems.
edibilityNote: Historically used as a cooking herb and still used to flavour foods; pennyroyal is toxic, and its concentrated oil can be fatal if swallowed.

summary: A bulbous flowering plant native to Spain and Portugal and naturalised in many other regions. It has narrow, rush-like leaves and bears clusters of scented yellow or white flowers in late spring. It has also been cultivated in France since the 18th century for perfume oil.

Tree with natural forms distributed across the Mediterranean Basin, parts of Africa and Arabia, Northwest India, Southwest China, Madeira and the Canary Islands. The species includes the cultivated olive and wild Mediterranean forms; one wild variety is smaller and shrubbier, with smaller leaves and fruit.
A grass native to northern Africa, western Asia and southern Europe, it has spikelets resembling those of the unrelated Bromus briziformis. Its seeds and leaves are edible.
edibilityNote: The seeds and leaves are edible.

summary: Grass native to southern Europe, northern Africa and southwestern Asia east to India. Its small stature, self-fertility and rapid life cycle make it a widely used experimental model for temperate grasses and cereal crops.

An annual grass native to the Mediterranean Basin, little quaking-grass forms narrow clumps of upright stems. Its flower clusters bear several small, cone-shaped spikelets that hang from slender stalks.

An annual or biennial grass native to northern Africa, western and central Asia, the Caucasus and much of Europe, barren brome has rough, hairy leaves that may be green or purplish. Its loose flower heads are open and nodding.

An annual grass native across Europe, North Africa and eastward to central Asia, sea barley grows mainly on bare coastal ground and inland salt flats. Its flower spikes break into fruit clusters dispersed by winter floods or livestock, and it thrives only where competition is limited.

A short, tuft-forming perennial grass widespread across much of Eurasia and North America. It has blue-green basal leaves and nearly cylindrical flower heads bearing shiny tan spikelets, sometimes tinged purple.
edibilityNote: The seed can be ground into powder and boiled as porridge or made into flour or bread.

summary: A stout perennial bunch grass originating from southern Europe and the Caucasus. It has grayish-blue leaves and dense, spike-like flower heads, eventually forming large bunches. Its alkaloids are implicated in livestock toxicity.

A perennial grass native to most of Europe and northern and western Asia. Timothy grows in tufts without runners, bears dense cylindrical flower heads with purple stamens, and tolerates cold and drought.

An annual bunchgrass native to North Africa, Europe and South Asia, lesser canary grass grows in tufts and bears spike-like flower clusters. It is widely naturalised elsewhere and is used for livestock forage and birdseed, although it is poisonous to some mammals.

An annual grass native to the Old World, it now occurs worldwide as an introduced species and sometimes a noxious weed. Its dense, greenish flower head looks soft and feathery because the spikelets bear long, fine, whitish bristles.
An annual or biennial plant native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, clustered dock has also been introduced to North America.
An annual or sometimes biennial herb native to Europe. It grows in wet places such as irrigation ditches, with shiny yellow flowers followed by spherical clusters of spiny fruits.

An evergreen shrub native from California to northern Mexico, it has yellow-green flowers without petals and red berries containing two nutlets. Native Americans in the western United States ate the fruit, though large quantities reportedly turned the body red.
edibilityNote: Native Americans in the western United States ate the fruit; large quantities reportedly gave the consumer's body a red tint.

summary: A dense deciduous shrub native to western North America, Pacific ninebark has reddish-gray bark that peels away in many thin layers. Its dark green leaves resemble grape or maple leaves, while creamy white flower clusters appear from late spring into midsummer.

An evergreen or deciduous shrub native from southern Europe and the Caucasus to parts of western Asia, scarlet firethorn has sharply thorned stems. It bears clusters of white flowers followed by small, bright red fruit.

A deciduous tree native to northeastern and central China and Taiwan, tree-of-heaven grows rapidly and spreads aggressively by seeds and root sprouts. All parts have a strong smell, often compared with peanuts or rotting cashews, and the tree can quickly recolonize after cutting.
edibilityNote: Roots are poisonous to humans; illness has also been reported after ingesting other plant parts or water contaminated by flowers.

summary: A perennial flowering herb native from Macaronesia and North Africa through Europe and Central Asia to the central Himalaya. Its sprawling reddish stems bear sticky blackish fruits, while its windblown pollen is a major cause of asthma and rhinitis around the Mediterranean.

Perennial herb native to the Mediterranean region. It bears numerous pink or red flowers, rarely white, in dense clusters and often grows on cliffs, rocks and walls. Its strongly scented leaves may be eaten raw in salads or cooked as vegetables.
edibilityNote: Leaves may be eaten raw in salads or cooked as vegetables, though their strong aroma may be unappealing.

summary: An annual herb native to southern and central Europe and western Asia. Its hairy climbing stems use leaf-tip tendrils for support, and it bears yellow or purple-marked pea-like flowers followed by hairy pods.

Annual flowering herb native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa. Its leaves have several pairs of narrow leaflets, and it bears solitary flowers or clusters of up to three with yellow or purple-tinged petals.

An erect annual crop whose wild ancestor and origin are unknown, the fava bean has square stems and grey-green leaves without climbing tendrils. Its white flowers have true-black wing spots. The beans are widely eaten, but people with favism must avoid them; boiling for ten minutes destroys most of their relatively low toxin levels.
edibilityNote: Beans are eaten raw or cooked; young pods and leaves are also edible. People with favism must avoid them, while boiling reduces most lectin toxins.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, lentil vetch has pale-blue flowers and leaves ending in a simple tendril. Its pods typically contain four seeds. In mainland Portugal it was assessed as regionally extinct after not being recorded since 1883.

summary: An annual legume believed to have originated in the Middle East, yellow vetchling has yellow flowers, sometimes streaked with violet. Its true leaves are reduced to tendrils, while leaf-like structures take their place.
edibilityNote: The fruits are eaten in parts of South Asia and may supplement grain diets, but large quantities are narcotic and potentially toxic.

summary: A perennial native to west-central and southern United States and Mexico. It grows mainly in subtropical regions.

summary: Legume native to parts of Europe and western Asia. It is grown for forage, winter ground cover and green manure, but its hard seeds and early seed shedding can leave it as a field weed.

An evergreen cashew-family tree native to arid and Andean South America. Its upper branches droop, and its bark, leaves and berries are aromatic when crushed; dense fruit clusters turn from green to red, pink or purple and may remain year-round. The berries are sold as pink peppercorns, although the fruit has caused vomiting and diarrhea in children and lacks US GRAS status.
edibilityNote: Pink/red berries are sold as peppercorns; extracts flavour drinks, while Wari and Inca fruit preparations included fermented drinks, syrup and maize gruel.

summary: A perennial shrub native to North America, it is thornless and has leaves made up of many hairy, oval leaflets. Its flower spikes feature single purple petals and prominent yellow-tipped stamens, followed by pods containing one or two seeds.
An evergreen shrub native to the Pacific coast of North America, it has large, long-lasting leaves and usually pink flowers. It contains a toxin that can poison honey from nearby hives.

A bulbous perennial native to southern and western France, Portugal and Spain, the hoop-petticoat daffodil has grass-like leaves and deep yellow flowers in mid-spring. Its unusually large central trumpet is surrounded by tiny pointed segments.
A rhizomatous flowering perennial native to Europe and temperate Asia. Arching leafy stems carry hanging white tubular flowers with green tips, and the plant can spread through shady areas.

An annual flowering plant native to the Iberian Peninsula and northwest Africa, Linaria amethystea has bluish-green stems and violet hairs on its upper leaf surfaces. Its spring flowers are usually amethyst-blue and white, with two lips and a long spur, although some subspecies have yellow flowers.

A perennial shrub endemic to Madeira, it inhabits some ravines in the island’s laurel forest. It has woody, hairy branches, heart-shaped leaves and usually dense clusters of orange-brown flowers, which appear from May to June.
A hairy perennial herb native to Western Europe and Tunisia. Its pale green or yellowish flowers face one side, lack an upper lip and bloom from June through August.
Edible perennial grassland herb native to Europe and Asia. It has square stems, purplish-red flower spikes and persistent tuberous runners that help it spread.
edibilityNote: Described as edible, with no particular part or preparation specified.

summary: A rhizomatous perennial orchid native across Europe, Asia and North Africa, it grows mainly in light or damp woodland. Its white, yellow-lipped flowers usually open only during the warmest, brightest hours, and some individuals lack green pigment and obtain all their nutrition from fungi.

A perennial twining herb of unstated native origin, hedge bindweed has a subcosmopolitan temperate distribution. It climbs counter-clockwise, bearing arrowhead-shaped leaves and white, sometimes pale-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers.
edibilityNote: The plant is toxic and contains calystegine alkaloids.

summary: A Mediterranean perennial found in sandy and stony places on limestone. It is sticky and glandular, woody at the base, and bears yellow flowers marked with reddish-brown stripes from April to July.
edibilityNote: Its branches are used in raisin preparation, but the source does not state that they are eaten.

summary: Evergreen partly parasitic shrub native to Europe and western and southern Asia. It grows on tree stems and produces white or yellow berries with very sticky pulp. Concentrated tea may be fatal and berries can cause serious illness, although mistletoe is an ingredient in Istrian biska liquor.
edibilityNote: An ingredient in Istrian biska liquor; concentrated infusions can be fatal, and berries have caused serious illness.

summary: Perennial thistle native to western and central Mediterranean regions, with a native presence in Portugal. It has violet-purple flower heads with fleshy receptacles and green-purple bracts ending in spines; its natural milk-coagulating effect is used in cheesemaking.
edibilityNote: Its natural milk-coagulating effect is used to make cheeses such as Serra da Estrela and Nisa.

summary: A flowering orchid of the Palaearctic and North Africa, the lesser butterfly-orchid has two shining green basal leaves. Its slim flower spike carries white, yellow-green-tinged flowers that are scented at night.

summary: An annual herb native from the Canary Islands across Europe to northern Iran and southern Turkmenistan, the dwarf violet grows in disturbed or grazed soil. It remains very short and bears characteristically asymmetrical violet flowers.

Spring-flowering bulbous perennial native to the western Iberian Peninsula, excluding the far northwest. Compared with the common bluebell, it has larger, paler and less drooping flowers, broader leaves, blue anthers and little or no scent; pink- and white-flowered forms also occur.

A fern indigenous to Asia, southern Europe, tropical Africa and Australia. It often grows around limestone or in cracks in concrete structures. It absorbs unusually high levels of arsenic and is used to clean polluted sites.

A bushy perennial flowering plant native to southern Europe and also present in southwest Asia and North Africa. It is a low, glandular-hairy plant with mostly three-part leaves and yellow flowers crowded among the leaves, growing in dry grassland and rocky places.

summary: An annual, sometimes biennial, flowering herb native to Europe, Africa and western Asia. Its small flowers have yellow anthers and are about half the diameter of those of the similar Geranium robertianum.

A bushy evergreen perennial native to woodland locations in Europe, Turkey and the Caucasus, wood spurge has slightly hairy dark-green leaves and green-yellow flower clusters in late spring and early summer. It thrives in dry tree shade and spreads rapidly through underground stems; its milky sap is toxic and irritates skin.
A large perennial subshrub native only to Madeira. It usually has a candelabra-like shape, densely hairy leaves and elongated clusters of blue or purple flowers that attract bees and butterflies.

Rhizomatous perennial native to China, Korea and Myanmar. It forms spreading clumps and usually bears blue to violet flowers with darker markings around a fringed white crest; a white form also exists.
edibilityNote: Most parts, including the rhizomes and leaves, are poisonous if ingested and may cause stomach pain and vomiting.

summary: Red alga with no stated native origin, widely found on moderately sheltered rocky shores around Europe. This small, tufted seaweed can vary from yellow-buff through red to almost black and never grows below low tide.
edibilityNote: Harvested and dried in Scotland and the Channel Islands as a curry-flavoured spice; also used in gin-making in northwestern Ireland.

summary: Marine red alga native to southern Australia and New Zealand. Its sparse branches bear long creeping stems with harpoon-like hooks, while mature plants form dense, intertwined pink clumps whose barbs attach to the seabed.

Perennial flowering plant native to northern Argentina, southern Brazil and Uruguay. It has pink-to-violet flowers and rosettes of three heart-shaped leaflets, whose undersides usually show orange granules. Thick, woody rhizomes allow it to spread into colonies.
edibilityNote: Rich in ascorbic acid and eaten as a vegetable by people in Jharkhand, India.

summary: Bulbous perennial from woods and meadows of the eastern Mediterranean, from Greece and Turkey to the Caucasus, including Armenia. It has simple basal leaves and short stems bearing mainly purple or blue flowers, though some varieties are white or pale pink. It blooms in mid-spring, and some selections are fragrant.

An aquatic perennial herb native to northern temperate and some subtropical regions of Europe, northwest Africa and western Asia. It has floating and submerged leaves and fragrant, solitary yellow flowers. It has been used as food since prehistoric times.
edibilityNote: Documented as food from prehistoric times; the supplied information does not identify particular edible parts or preparations.

summary: An annual herb native to Europe, western Asia and northern Africa. Its sometimes-climbing stems carry white or cream flowers tipped with purple, which gradually turn pink after pollination.

A short-lived perennial flowering plant reported as native across the Old World from southern Africa to Eurasia. It is semi-aquatic, with pale violet-blue flower spikes, and can spread when flood-broken pieces root downstream.

A tufted perennial sedge of unstated native origin, it is widespread across higher latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere. It forms tight clumps in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor bogs and bears white flower clusters in August, followed by dry fruits with beak-like caps.

summary: Small herbaceous plant found in Australia and New Zealand, mainly on hillsides and in weedy areas. It is New Zealand’s smallest Oxalis species, with leaves ranging from green to purple.

A perennial aquatic plant found nearly worldwide in freshwater habitats. It forms dense floating mats of small green discs with dark-red undersides, and rarely flowers. It is hardly used for human nutrition and is not cultivated for it because of contamination, heavy-metal and calcium-oxalate concerns.
edibilityNote: Hardly used for human nutrition and not cultivated for it because of contamination, heavy-metal and calcium-oxalate concerns.

summary: An annual flowering herb native to the tropical Americas. It branches freely, and larger plants become tumbleweeds after dying and drying; in Cambodia, its leaves are sometimes cooked and eaten by people.
edibilityNote: In Cambodia, the leaves are sometimes cooked and eaten by people.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to Macaronesia and Europe’s Atlantic, Baltic and Mediterranean coasts. It grows in salty, sandy coastal soils and was historically burned to produce soda ash for glassmaking.

A perennial herb naturally found from eastern Europe across central and eastern Asia, extending south to northern India and Mexico; its North American presence may reflect prehistoric human introduction from Asia. Its small, narrow leaves taste sweet and mildly spicy and are used fresh or dried as seasoning.
edibilityNote: Leaves are used fresh or dried in pickles, stews, salads, béarnaise sauce, vinegars and other culinary infusions.

summary: Annual flowering plant whose native origin is unresolved in the supplied information. Its female flower heads become buoyant, hooked burs that catch in animal hair. Small amounts of mature plant parts may be consumed, but seeds and seedlings should not be eaten in large quantities because they contain an extremely toxic chemical.
edibilityNote: Small amounts of mature parts may be consumed; seeds, seedlings and large quantities are dangerous, and famine consumption caused deaths in Bangladesh in 2007.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to the Mediterranean regions of Europe and Africa. Its leaves are dotted with resin, and the structures surrounding its flower heads end in spines.

An annual flowering herb of unknown native origin, possibly from South America and perhaps Chile, it is now a widespread weed of disturbed ground. Long, yellowish three-pronged spines grow near the leaf forks, while hooked burs spread by attaching to animals, people and objects or floating on water.

Perennial herb native to the Americas and northern Australia. It has fleshy stems and thick leaves, with coiled double rows of small white flowers whose throats may be purple or yellow. It commonly grows in salty soils such as beaches, alkali flats and salt marshes.

A winter annual herb native to the Middle East, North Africa and southern Europe, it commonly occupies dry, disturbed ground. Developing seedpods rise above its compact yellow flower heads. Its spicy leaves, seeds and flowers are edible, while cured pods can be parched, ground into meal and cooked in soup or stew.
edibilityNote: Leaves, seeds and flowers are eaten; cured pods can be parched, ground into meal and made into soup or stew.

summary: An annual flowering herb native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, eastern rocket has a hairy, branching stem. Its lower leaves are deeply divided, while pale yellow flowers at the stem tips develop into long, narrow fruits.
Annual flowering herb native to Eurasia and North Africa. Its creeping stems are coated with small, fuzzy, pale green leaves, and its flowers have hairy green sepals but no petals.

Low-lying shrub of the southwestern United States, California, Idaho and northern Mexico; its native status is not specified. It grows in sandy, often salty and strongly alkaline ground, with fleshy, knobby green stems, scale-like leaves and seeds used as food in prehistoric North America.
edibilityNote: The seeds were used as food in prehistoric North America.

summary: A fast-growing annual whose native range is obscure but reportedly spans temperate Eurasia, the Indian subcontinent, North Africa, Ethiopia, and the eastern and central United States. Its lower leaves are toothed and roughly diamond-shaped, while upper leaves have a whitish, mealy underside. Young shoots may be eaten raw or cooked; leaves, flower buds and flowers are preferably cooked, and the seeds also have traditional food uses.
edibilityNote: Young shoots may be raw or cooked; leaves, flower buds and flowers are cooked. Seeds have traditional food and drink uses.

summary: A perennial herb native to Eurasia and parts of Africa, it has branching stems that root at their joints and form spreading patches. Its round flowerheads change from white to pink, then develop pinkish, net-patterned fruit clusters resembling strawberries.

Annual flowering plant native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico. Its wild form is hairy and glandular, with intricately divided, lacy leaves and coiling clusters of blue or lavender flowers. Its seeds germinate only in darkness.

A herbaceous perennial native to temperate Europe, western and central Asia, the Himalaya, eastern Siberia and North America, corn mint spreads by creeping rootstocks. It has hairy, coarsely toothed leaves and pale purple flowers, occasionally white or pink, clustered around the stems. Its leaves can be eaten raw or made into tea.
edibilityNote: The leaves can be eaten raw or made into tea, traditionally to treat colds or aid digestion.

summary: Aromatic evergreen shrub native to the southern coastal mountain ranges of California and Baja California. Its spring-green leaves mature to grayish white, while arching branches may root where they touch the ground. Tight clusters of pinkish-purple flowers rise on similarly coloured stems.

Annual or perennial herb native to northern Africa, southern Europe, and western and central Asia. It has broad, shallow-lobed leaves and small white or pink flowers, and the entire plant is eaten raw or cooked with a mild, chard-like flavour.
edibilityNote: The entire plant is eaten raw or cooked and has a mild flavour resembling chard.

summary: A small deciduous tree or large shrub native to the south-central United States. Its bumpy yellow-green fruit releases sticky white latex when damaged, while its strong, flexible, durable wood was traditionally prized for bows.
edibilityNote: The fruit is generally not eaten by humans and is mostly inedible; its seeds are called edible, but only squirrel use is documented.

summary: A small to medium-sized tree native to eastern Australia, it often has a crooked trunk and a domed canopy of greyish foliage. Its bark may be fibrous below and smooth, mottled grey, cream and yellow above; groups of seven buds produce white flowers in the Australian spring.
Tree native to eastern Australia and southern New Guinea. It has smooth bark mottled white, grey and blue as irregular sheets are shed, along with white flowers and woody, hemispherical fruit.

Plantain native to the Mediterranean region and naturalized in parts of Asia and North America. Its ground seed husks are an indigestible source of soluble dietary fiber and are widely used in commercial psyllium products.
edibilityNote: Ground seed husks are consumed as indigestible soluble dietary fiber in commercial psyllium products.

summary: A large deciduous plane tree native to California and Baja California, especially waterways, canyons and floodplains. Its bark forms a striking patchwork of pale colours, while its broad lobed leaves turn golden to orange-red before falling.

A deciduous willow native to dry areas of northern China, Korea, Mongolia, Japan and Siberia. It grows rapidly but is short-lived, with narrow leaves that turn golden yellow in autumn. Its strongly drooping form is a cultivated selection.

A deciduous tree native to China, Korea and Manchuria, the golden rain tree has a broad, dome-shaped crown. Large end clusters of yellow flowers are followed by inflated, bladder-like pods that ripen from green to orange and pink in autumn.

A poisonous herbaceous perennial native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico, sacred datura bears sweetly fragrant white trumpet flowers and spiny round seed capsules. All parts contain dangerous alkaloids and may be fatal if eaten, with the roots considered the most potent part.
edibilityNote: All parts may be fatal if eaten; the roots are considered the most potent and alkaloid-rich part.

summary: Flowering shrub or small tree native to South America and introduced widely elsewhere. It has smooth, bluish-green, rubbery leaves and yellow tubular flowers; every part is potentially poisonous to people and livestock.
edibilityNote: Poisonous cooked or raw; ingesting the leaves can be fatal because they contain high levels of anabasine and nicotine.

summary: A bushy annual herb endemic to the western United States, it bears white, greenish or purple-tinged flowers with long tubular throats. Indigenous peoples traditionally cultivated it along parts of the western coast and the middle Columbia River.
A flowering wetland plant whose native origin is not specified. Sea clubrush grows widely in coastal and inland saline wetlands, often dominating mineral-rich mud where water levels fluctuate.

Flowering plant native to southern California and Baja California, chaparral yucca forms a stemless rosette of rigid, sharp-pointed, finely toothed leaves. Its single flower stalk grows extremely quickly and carries hundreds of fragrant white to purplish flowers; the flowering shoot usually dies afterward, while most subspecies produce basal offshoots. Before European settlement, Native Americans ground its seeds into flour and ate pit-roasted hearts, roasted stalks and often parboiled petals.
edibilityNote: Before European settlement, Native Americans ground seeds into flour, pit-roasted hearts, roasted slightly bitter stalks and often parboiled petals.

summary: A winter annual grass native to Europe, southwestern Asia and northern Africa. Its hairy leaves and drooping flower clusters are distinctive. It readily invades disturbed ground and spreads through rapid growth and prolific seed production.

A warm-season grass native to Europe, Africa, Australia and much of Asia, Bermuda grass spreads by creeping stems and underground rhizomes, forming dense mats. It has deep roots, recovers quickly from damage and produces durable turf in hot, dry regions.

Annual grass native to the Mediterranean Basin and neighbouring regions, from Portugal and the Canary Islands east to Ethiopia and northern India. It has conspicuous clusters of golden flowers and favours dry, stony places in Portugal; it is naturalized in parts of Australia and the Americas, sometimes as an invasive weed.

summary: A grass native to Eurasia and North Africa, it forms dense clumps with swollen stem bases, especially in drier places. It rarely produces viable seed and usually reproduces through these detachable bases and bulbils held in green, leaflike flower clusters.

A flowering grass whose native origin is not specified, it occurs in tropical regions. It has tall, thick stems, long leaves and pyramid-shaped flower clusters that bloom in the first year. It may be grown as an annual or perennial.

A perennial herb found throughout tropical and subtropical regions worldwide, it thrives in marshes and other wetlands and can tolerate highly saline water. In southern Iraq’s Mesopotamian Marshes, its pollen is reportedly made into a dessert called khirret, though the source flags this claim as needing a full citation.
edibilityNote: In southern Iraq, its pollen is reportedly made into khirret dessert; the source marks this claim as needing a full citation.

summary: An aromatic annual herb probably originating in western and central Asia. Its white or lilac flowers usually appear from July to September, and its delicately aromatic, spicy flavour is valued as a culinary seasoning.
edibilityNote: Used as a culinary seasoning; in Bulgarian cuisine it is mixed with salt and paprika to make sharena sol.

summary: An evergreen pine native to Eurasia, Scots pine is readily recognized by its short blue-green needles and orange-red bark. Mature trees often have a long, bare, straight trunk topped by a rounded or flat mass of foliage.

summary: An evergreen conifer with a Holarctic distribution across the cool temperate Northern Hemisphere, common juniper varies from a small tree to a ground-hugging shrub. It has needle-like leaves in threes and berry-like cones that ripen over 18 months from green to waxy blue-black. The bitter cones are not eaten raw; dried and usually crushed, they flavour meats, sauces, stuffings, beer and gin.
edibilityNote: Bitter cones are not eaten raw; they are dried, usually crushed, and used sparingly to flavour foods, beers and spirits.

summary: A small deciduous shrub native to Japan and eastern Asia. It has spiny brown branches, pale yellow spring flowers, leaves that turn red in autumn, and glossy red-to-orange edible berries that persist through winter. It is widely naturalized in China and North America and invasive in many places.
edibilityNote: The glossy red-to-orange berry is edible and matures from late summer through autumn.

summary: A crabapple tree native to China, it bears white flowers and yellow or red fruit. Some varieties are grown for their fruit.
edibilityNote: Some varieties are grown for their fruit.

summary: A deciduous shrub native to southern Ontario and the eastern United States, silky dogwood bears opposite oval leaves and small blue fruits. Its rusty-brown twigs can spread into dense thickets, particularly in wetland habitats.

A floating aquatic fern native to warm-temperate and tropical regions of the Americas. Its tiny branching plants may be green with pink, orange or red edges and can rapidly cover an entire lake surface. It largely dies back during temperate winters but survives through submerged buds.

A perennial fern native to places including Finland, brittle bladderfern grows mainly in shady, slightly moist rocky cracks and ledges. Its leaves are finely divided, with many rounded spore clusters underneath.
An annual plant believed native to the central and possibly eastern United States, procumbent pigweed has smooth, hairless surfaces. It flowers from summer into fall.
edibilityNote: Several Native American groups ate the seeds; Zuni people initially ate them raw and later ground them with black cornmeal and formed them into balls.

summary: An annual flowering herb that may be native to the Neotropics or central and eastern North America, redroot amaranth is now introduced across most continents. It can form a tumbleweed and bears dense flower clusters threaded with spiny green bracts.
edibilityNote: Leaves, stems, young shoots and seeds are eaten raw or cooked; discard boiling water because leaves contain oxalic acid and may contain nitrates.

summary: A strongly scented herb native across much of Eurasia, Macaronesia and North Africa, celery grows naturally in damp, often salty places. Cultivated forms are vegetables selected for edible leaf stalks, swollen stem bases, or leaves and stems, which may be eaten raw or cooked.
edibilityNote: Wild celery was historically a condiment; cultivated forms provide raw or cooked stalks, swollen stem bases, leaves and stems.

summary: Waterside carrot-family plant of unspecified native origin, widespread across much of Europe, Asia, Australia and North America. Its hollow stems bear thread-like leaves underwater and broader leaves above water, while crushed stalks smell of carrot or parsnip. The Zuni use it in schumaakwe cakes.
edibilityNote: The Zuni people use the plant as an ingredient in schumaakwe cakes.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: An aquatic plant native to North America and parts of South America. It floats or creeps in wet, sandy places and has rounded leaves; it is eaten in salads or cooked as a pot herb.
edibilityNote: Used raw in salads or cooked as a pot herb.

summary: A perennial herb native to mountainous and wooded parts of California and Arizona, it is hairy and aromatic. Its narrow fruits are ribbed and bristly, while its tiny flowers are greenish yellow.

A flowering plant native to southern Africa, brass buttons spreads stems along the ground and raises bright yellow, button-like flower heads. It is highly salt-tolerant and favours muddy wetlands and brackish habitats, with fleshy leaves and reddish stems.

A branching subshrub native to southern Europe, North Africa and western Asia as far east as Pakistan. It smells of camphor and has narrow leaves coated in sticky resin. The resin can cause allergic reactions and severe dermatitis, so gloves are advised when handling it.

A flowering plant native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico, telegraphweed is tall, bristly and glandular. Its hairy, toothed or lobed leaves become smaller up the stem, ending in bright yellow, daisy-like flower heads and later spherical seed heads with long white tufts.

Annual herb native to parts of Europe, the Mediterranean, the Middle East and the Indian subcontinent. It sprawls through disturbed, shady ground, with many-branched stems and loose clusters of small flowers.

A fast-growing annual herb widespread in North America, with toothed lower leaves and seeds marked by distinctive honeycomb-like pits. It was cultivated by Indigenous peoples in prehistoric North America and remains a crop in Mexico.
edibilityNote: Leaves, young shoots and seeds are eaten; cooking reduces oxalic acid, and seeds are soaked and rinsed to remove saponins.

summary: A small succulent native to Eurasia, particularly the Mediterranean Basin. Its fleshy foliage changes from green through orange to deep red as it matures, and tiny flowers appear between opposite pairs of pointed leaves.

A fast-growing annual plant native to North America. Its spreading stems form ground-hugging mats, and its small hairy leaves usually bear a central brown spot. Broken leaves or stems release poisonous milky sap that can irritate skin and cause stomach irritation and vomiting if swallowed.
edibilityNote: The poisonous milky sap has been ingested medicinally as a laxative or to induce vomiting, but can irritate the stomach and cause vomiting.

summary: An annual or biennial legume native to much of Asia, southern Europe and northeastern Africa. Its small white flowers form narrow, often drooping clusters, and the whole plant has a sweet scent that intensifies when dried.

An annual or biennial flowering herb native to Europe, it commonly grows in moist places such as marshes, wet fields and rice paddies. Its branching stems carry spikes of small pinkish flowers followed by oval capsules containing many minute seeds.

Annual-to-perennial herb native to Eurasia and North Africa. Its narrow leaves form a ground-level rosette and are toothed or deeply divided, resembling a buck’s horn. The leaves are grown as a vegetable, especially for salad mixes.
edibilityNote: Leaves are cultivated as a vegetable called erba stella, mainly for salad mixes.

summary: A herbaceous perennial native to Eurasia and temperate Africa, greater plantain forms a broad leaf rosette and narrow flower spikes bearing many small, bitter seeds. Young tender leaves are eaten in salads, older leaves can be stewed, and the seeds can be ground as a flour substitute or extender.
edibilityNote: Young leaves are eaten raw; older leaves are cooked in stews. The tiny seeds can be ground as a flour substitute or extender.

summary: A prostrate annual-to-perennial herb considered native in most places and on every continent except Antarctica, but introduced in Venezuela and the Falkland Islands and absent from southern Asia. It inhabits springs, streams and seasonally wet grassland, sometimes forming mats or floating. In Spain and Portugal, wild plants are gathered and eaten as salad, though they are not cultivated.
edibilityNote: Wild plants are gathered for salad in Spain and Portugal but are not currently cultivated.

summary: Succulent plant of unclear native origin, now ranging from North Africa and southern Europe through Asia to Australasia; much of this spread is assumed to be human-assisted, and its status in the Americas is uncertain. It has reddish, mostly ground-hugging stems and small yellow flowers that open briefly on sunny mornings. All parts are edible raw or cooked, and the seeds can be eaten or made into flour, though the leaves contain high oxalate levels.
edibilityNote: All parts are edible raw or cooked; seeds are also eaten raw or made into flour.

summary: An annual herb native to the Mediterranean Basin, parts of the Middle East and nearby Atlantic islands, tiny bedstraw has very short upright stems with small leaves arranged in whorls. Its tiny greenish flowers grow singly or in pairs, followed by fruits covered in hooked hairs.

An annual herb native to the Mediterranean area and Western Europe, including northern Africa, Turkey, Iran and eastern North Atlantic islands. Its thin, branching stems carry rings of narrow leaves and tiny greenish-white or purple-tinged flowers; hooked bristles densely cover the fruit. It readily occupies rocky habitats and old stone walls.
A semiaquatic annual flowering herb native to much of the temperate world. It forms low fleshy tufts in mud or wet sand, with spoon-shaped leaves and tiny white flowers sometimes tinted pink or blue.

summary: A flowering biennial native to Eurasia and North Africa, moth mullein forms a basal leaf rosette in its first year and a slender flowering stem in its second. Its yellow or white flowers have orange stamens covered in purple hairs, resembling moth antennae. It has naturalized widely in North America and is considered invasive there.

A hairy biennial herb native to Europe, northern Africa and Asia. It forms a large leaf rosette followed by a tall stem densely packed with small yellow flowers. Its abundant seeds may remain able to germinate for decades.

A flowering plant of unspecified native origin, turkey tangle frogfruit occurs across tropical regions worldwide and is often grown as ground cover. Its flower heads have a purple centre ringed by small white-to-pink flowers, giving them a match-like appearance.

An annual sedge native to southern Europe, most of Africa and Asia, and Australia. It grows in wet habitats and rice fields, with thin stems, wispy basal leaves and rounded clusters containing many tiny brown flowers.

Tufted herbaceous sedge native to subtropical and tropical South America. It has a short woody rhizome and umbrella-like clusters of small flowers. In some regions, people eat its nut-like tubers raw or cooked, and the stem base is also edible.
edibilityNote: In some regions, the small nut-like tubers are eaten raw or cooked; the stem base is also edible.

summary: A herbaceous emergent plant of unspecified native origin, three-square bulrush is widespread across much of the Americas, Europe, New Zealand and Australia. This long-lived marsh perennial has rough, dense dark-green foliage and small flowers in compact spikelets.

A tiny duckweed native to parts of the Americas, though its exact native range is unknown, least duckweed is the smallest Lemna species. Its translucent green body grows singly in shade and usually in pairs in full sun, and it produces a short-lived flower.

Duckweed native to much of the Americas, Valdivia duckweed is a minute flowering plant that forms mats on calm freshwater. Its flat, translucent, pale green body produces a root and a tiny, short-lived flower, often enclosed in a membrane.

A tufted grass native to much of northern North America and most widespread in the west, western fescue usually grows in forests and woodlands. It has hairlike basal leaves, does not spread through underground stems, and flowers from late June into July.

An aquatic perennial native to Eurasia and the Americas, longleaf pondweed grows in ponds, lakes, ditches and streams. Its submerged leaves are narrow while its floating leaves are oval, and both types are carried on notably long stalks.
Flowering grass native to mainland Portugal and Madeira, but introduced to São Miguel and Terceira in the Azores. Its reddish colour is a distinctive feature.

A clump-forming perennial native to Europe, chives have dark-green rounded leaves and pale-pink, pompom-like flowers. Their mild onion-flavoured fresh leaves and stems are used raw in salads and as seasoning in many dishes.
edibilityNote: Fresh leaves and stems are eaten raw or used as seasoning in salads, soups, potatoes and egg or cheese dishes.

summary: Herbaceous flowering plant placed in the asparagus family by modern phylogenetic classifications.

A small herbaceous perennial found in Europe, the eastern Mediterranean and North Africa, ground-pine resembles a tiny pine tree. Its three-lobed leaves smell like pine needles when crushed, and its seeds can remain alive in soil for up to 50 years.

An annual or biennial herb native to central and southern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, field marigold has bright yellow to orange flower heads on slender, hairy stems. Its fruits occur in three shapes, including ring-shaped forms.

Annual herbaceous plant recorded from North Africa, the Mediterranean region, western Asia and Ukraine. It has soft shaggy hairs, yellow flowers and hanging pods with upturned tips resembling a bird's foot; at night, its flower clusters bend beneath raised, folded leaves.
