summary: Annual wild pea native to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. It has branched curling tendrils and single flowers in varying shades of red.
edibilityNote: Historically eaten as cicerchia in Milan in 1288, although the species is known to cause lathyrism.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to the Mediterranean region. Garden forms range from yellow flowers surrounded by sea-green leafy bracts to purple flowers with blue bracts; in Europe it flowers from May to August.
A perennial flowering herb endemic to the Mediterranean basin, broad-leaved anemone has fragrant solitary flowers ranging from bluish white or mauve to red-purple. It flowers from March through May.
An annual herb whose native origin is not stated in the supplied information. It is a small, self-supporting plant with broad compound leaves.

A herbaceous annual native to disturbed ground in Europe and naturalized as a weed elsewhere, including North America. Its pink flowers resemble miniature snapdragons, followed by hairy green fruit said to resemble a weasel's snout.

A flowering plant native to southern Europe and some Mediterranean islands, spring sowbread has wide, heart-shaped leaves that are often coarsely toothed or lobed. Its late-spring flowers have long, slender petals and may be deep carmine-pink or white.

Annual flowering herb native to temperate and boreal North America and Eurasia, usually growing beside ponds, streams and other wet ground. It has deeply divided, mostly hairless leaves and small yellow flowers. All parts are considered poisonous, and ingestion can cause burning, pain, tongue inflammation and increased salivation.
edibilityNote: All parts are considered poisonous; ingestion can irritate the skin and mucous membranes.

summary: Orchid native to the Mediterranean Basin, including parts of southern Europe, western Asia and northern Africa. Its dense bright-pink flower clusters appear in April, and each flower has a lobed lip resembling a naked person wearing a hat.
An orchid found widely across Europe and Asia, as far north as Germany. It grows in wet meadows with alkaline soil; mass flowering can occur in Jersey and Guernsey from late May to early June.

summary: A flowering orchid native to western Eurasia and northern Africa, the green-winged orchid usually bears purple flowers, though they may range from white to deep purple. Its green-veined side petals resemble wings, and its flowers produce no nectar.
Herbaceous orchid of Mediterranean distribution. Its dense flower clusters have pink to purple sepals and a paler pink central lip, sometimes marked with fan-like veins.

summary: A herbaceous perennial orchid native to Europe, northern Africa and western Asia. Its flowers resemble human figures, with petals and sepals forming the head and the divided lip forming a hanging torso and limbs; it usually grows in sunny, often calcareous grassland.
Terrestrial orchid native to the Mediterranean region from Portugal and Morocco to Turkey. Its flower is said to resemble a sawfly, though this resemblance is only purported.

An orchid native across the Mediterranean region from Portugal and the Canary Islands to Turkey and Lebanon, it has flowers resembling female Eucera bees in appearance and scent. Male bees attempting to mate with the flowers carry pollen between plants.

An orchid native to southern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, from Portugal and Morocco to Syria. Its flowers may be yellow or have blue-grey or brown velvety spots. Male Andrena bees pollinate it while facing away from the pollen structures, collecting pollen on their abdomen.

An annual herb native to Eurasia, it commonly grows as a weed in disturbed ground and has been introduced elsewhere. Long hairs and bristles cover the plant, including its sharply lobed leaves and the pointed structures surrounding its yellow flower heads.
Annual herb of unspecified native origin, with broad compound leaves. Its flowers are visited by several kinds of mason bee.

Bulb-growing wildflower native to western North America, from southwestern British Columbia to northern California. It has mottled basal leaves and nodding white flowers with yellow-based, upward-curving segments.
edibilityNote: Native Americans reportedly ate the roots raw or cooked; the source does not identify the groups or period.

summary: A perennial herb native to western North America, from southern Alaska and British Columbia south to Utah and California. Its hand-shaped leaves have numerous leaflets, while wild plants usually bear tall spikes of blue-to-purple flowers. Newer garden hybrids are highly poisonous and should never be eaten.
edibilityNote: Newer garden hybrids are highly poisonous and should never be eaten; low-alkaloid cultivars mentioned are bred for animal fodder.

summary: A small tree or shrub native to foothill woodlands and chaparral, the western redbud is found primarily in Oregon and Northern California. Its bright pink or magenta flowers emerge before the leaves, while clusters of thin, brown or reddish-purple pods persist through winter.

A coniferous tree native to scattered groves on the western slopes of California’s Sierra Nevada. Giant sequoias are the most massive individual trees on Earth, and the oldest known specimen lived for more than 3,200 years.
A biennial plant native to Europe. It has very large leaves and pink-to-purple flower heads whose hooked outer bracts attach to people and animals.
edibilityNote: Young leafstalks, leaves and flower stalks are eaten raw or cooked; roots require boiling with changed water and become woody after one year.

summary: A deciduous conifer native to the mountains of central Europe, with isolated lowland populations in northern Poland. Its light-green needles turn bright yellow before falling in autumn, and old cones may remain on the tree for years. A lifespan near 1,000 years is confirmed, while ages around 2,000 years are considered likely.

A grass native to the southeastern United States, Grenada, Central America and South America. Its folded or flat leaf blades have fine hairs along their edges and may turn purple or reddish when mature; it is often used as permanent pasture.

A root vegetable native to Eurasia, wild parsnip is related to carrot but is paler and more strongly flavoured. Its root and the part just above it are eaten cooked in stews and soups, while other plant parts are toxic. Cultivated since ancient times, it served as a staple before potatoes were introduced.
edibilityNote: The root and adjoining lower stem are eaten cooked; other plant parts are toxic.

summary: A flowering plant native to Eurasia, including central and western Europe. It forms a rosette of finely hairy leaves and bears delicate pink-white flowers from May to September.
edibilityNote: The plant is documented as edible; fresh leaves have reported nutritional values.

summary: A parasitic broomrape native to the Mediterranean basin in Europe and North Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, and Western Asia as far as Iran, bean broomrape commonly lives on faba beans. It lacks chlorophyll, and its stems are gathered and eaten in Apulia, southern Italy.
edibilityNote: Its stems are gathered and eaten in Apulia, southern Italy.

summary: An annual flowering herb native to the Mediterranean region, garland daisy has aromatic, deeply divided leaves and small yellow flower heads. Its greens are eaten in many Asian cuisines, while the stronger-tasting stalk can also be used; overcooking may make them bitter.
edibilityNote: Greens and stronger-tasting stalks are eaten, often simmered, steamed, stir-fried, deep-fried or added to soups; overcooking may make them bitter.

summary: Evergreen pine native to the southeastern United States, from eastern Texas to Florida and north to southern New Jersey. It has yellowish- to grayish-green needles in bundles of three, sometimes twisted, and older trees develop reddish-brown bark with deep fissures and broad, scaly plates.
An annual flowering herb endemic to California. Its spring flowers are bowl-shaped and white with dark veins, dots and a purple spot at each lobe tip.

A herbaceous perennial native to temperate parts of western Asia, Africa and Europe, the sand crocus has thin, narrow, often curled leaves. Its usually solitary pink, pale purple or violet flower has pointed petals, darker veins and a yellow or golden throat, blooming from February onward or between March and May.

A corm-forming iris-family plant native to the Mediterranean region—southern Europe, northern Africa and the Middle East—and Sudan. It has long, slender leaves and small six-part blooms; most varieties flower purple or violet, but some are white or yellow.
A rhizomatous evergreen perennial native to the Juan Fernández Islands, central and southern Chile, and southern Argentina.

A herbaceous perennial native to central and northwestern Europe, marsh gladiolus has sword-shaped leaves and rosy-violet or magenta flowers. Despite its name, it does not grow in marshes, preferring moist, lime-rich meadows and forest clearings that alternate between wet and dry.

Corm-forming herbaceous perennial native to temperate northern Africa, western Asia and southern Europe, from the Mediterranean to the Caucasus. It is a vigorous plant with linear leaves and bright pink flowers in spring.

A perennial herb native to western South Africa, growing from an underground corm. It has long, sword-shaped dark green leaves and curved tubular orange flowers from midwinter to early spring, pollinated by birds.

A herbaceous elder native to southern and central Europe and southwest Asia, dwarf elder forms large groups of upright stems from an extensive underground stem. It bears flat-topped clusters of white, occasionally pink, flowers and glossy black berries. All parts are toxic, especially the seeds, though cooking can neutralize the toxicity.
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic, especially the seeds, but cooking can neutralize the toxicity; explicit human food use is not described.

summary: A perennial herb native to western North America, silverleaf phacelia grows in habitats from scrub to forest, usually on sandy or rocky soil. Fine silvery hairs cover the plant, and its white or lavender flowers are urn- or bell-shaped.

Herbaceous perennial native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, where it is scarce within its range. It lacks chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise, instead drawing resources from fungal networks associated with trees; its fleshy, fungus-like growth may be yellow, red or yellowish-white.

summary: A biennial or short-lived perennial herb native to southern Europe and parts of Asia, sweet William bears dense clusters of spicy, clove-scented flowers. Wild flowers are red with white bases, while cultivated forms include white, pink, red, purple and patterned colours. Its flowers are considered edible, although the source marks this claim as needing a citation.
edibilityNote: The flowers are considered edible, but the supplied source flags this statement as needing a citation.

summary: Small herbaceous flowering plant native to central and southern Europe, Turkey, the Caucasus and Iran. Its wiry, branching stems bear narrow leaves and solitary pink-to-white flowers at their tips.

An erect annual flowering herb found in central Europe and southern European mountains. Its dense clusters of small pink or purple flowers are surrounded by brown papery bracts, and it grows in grasslands and beside roads.

A parasitic herb of European–Caucasian origin, occurring as an annual or sometimes a perennial. It lacks chlorophyll and draws nutrients from host roots, usually legumes; even its seeds require nearby host roots to germinate.

A non-photosynthetic parasitic flowering plant native to Southern Europe. Its colour varies widely from reddish or yellowish brown to purple or yellow, making identification by colour unreliable. It attaches to many hosts, especially plants in the pea and daisy families.

A plant in the Orobanchaceae family whose native origin is not stated. Its seeds attract wood ants, which carry and disperse them over short distances. It is also a food plant for heath fritillary caterpillars.

A flowering succulent native to South Africa’s southwestern Cape, deltoid-leaved dewplant has silver-blue, three-sided leaves with red-edged teeth and often purple-tinged stems. It produces masses of pink, almond-scented flowers in spring.
A succulent shrub whose native origin is not stated, orange dewplant has a self-supporting form and simple, broad leaves.
A trailing succulent perennial native to South Africa's Eastern Cape, it has hairy stems and small cylindrical or triangular leaves. Its flowers are lavender, pink or occasionally white.

A prostrate flowering succulent endemic to eastern Australia, angular sea-fig usually grows very close to the sea. It has blue-grey leaves, daisy-like light-purple to deep pinkish-purple flowers, and red to purple fruit that ripens mainly in summer and autumn.
edibilityNote: Aboriginal peoples ate the fruit; the fleshy leaves may be eaten raw or cooked, and roasted leaves can serve as a salt substitute.

summary: A creeping flowering plant found in North and South America and the West Indies. Its unusual leaves spread through marshy or wet ground, and it is widely used as a foreground aquarium plant.

A perennial flowering herb native to western North America from Alaska to California. It grows in wet places such as streambanks and is sometimes aquatic. Its parsley-like leaves are divided into serrated, lobed leaflets, and its many flowers have bright white to red-tinged petals.

An erect perennial herb widespread across much of North America, western ragweed also grows as an introduced plant elsewhere. Its hairy stems bear deeply divided leaves and flower spikes, while a creeping root system allows it to sprout as well as reproduce by seed.

A herbaceous perennial native to Europe, western Asia and northern Africa, creeping thistle forms extensive colonies from thick roots that send up many shoots. It has very spiny leaves and pink-purple flower heads, usually on separate male and female plants.
edibilityNote: Roots are rarely eaten and may cause flatulence; leaves and stalks are also edible, though spines make the leaves tedious to prepare.

summary: An annual or perennial flowering herb native to the United States, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and northern South America, marsh fleabane inhabits wetlands, coastal habitats and moist inland sites, often on salty ground. It is strongly aromatic and roughly hairy, with toothed oval leaves and clusters of bright pinkish-purple or magenta flower heads.
edibilityNote: In parts of the Caribbean, the leaves are consumed as medicinal tea; use is discouraged during pregnancy and advised in moderation.

summary: A low-growing annual herb native to South America, common soliva has small parsley-like leaves and upward-pointing clusters of tiny, sharp seeds. These seeds make infested ground painful for barefoot people and are also avoided by dogs and cats.

Perennial mustard-family plant native to southern Europe, Mediterranean countries and Asia east to the Himalayas. It has waxy leaves, small white flowers and an extensive deep root network. Its leaves, shoots and fruits are edible; in Ladakh, young growth is boiled and soaked to remove bitterness before being cooked like spinach.
edibilityNote: Leaves, shoots and fruits are edible; in Ladakh, young growth is boiled, soaked for two days and cooked like spinach.

summary: A small perennial herb native to southern South America. Its sprawling stems have woody bases and glandular hairs, while its flowers bear hairy sepals and five whitish petals.

A circumboreal annual herb that has become naturalized across many temperate regions. It has spreading branches and diamond-shaped leaves, and accumulates environmental salt in its tissues. Its young leaves and shoots can be eaten raw or cooked as a bland spinach substitute.
edibilityNote: Young leaves and shoots are edible raw or cooked and can serve as a bland spinach substitute.

summary: A flowering saltbush native to Europe, Macaronesia, northern Africa, Ethiopia, the Middle East, western Siberia and Central Asia. It can live in salty environments but does not depend on them.

A perennial herb endemic to Australia and native to Western Australia, South Australia, Queensland and New South Wales. It often forms low mats from a woody taproot and produces succulent fruit structures that turn red or orange when mature.

A clover native to Europe, southwest Asia, northwest Africa and Macaronesia. Unlike other clovers, it develops its seeds underground, and it can thrive in poor soil where other clovers cannot survive.

Perennial flowering aquatic plant native to the Amazon River in South America. Its feathery blue-green to waxy grey-green leaves grow in whorls, while distinctive stems and leaves emerge above the water like small fir trees. It can spread from fragments and form dense surface mats.
Herbaceous annual native to Europe. It has been introduced across almost every region of the United States and Canada, where it is associated with disturbed sites.

An annual flowering herb native to most of the contiguous United States except the Pacific Northwest and New England. It grows in moist places, with green to deep-red linear leaves and small rose-to-lavender flowers clustered at the upper leaf joints.

An annual plant native to Central and East Asia. It has large heart-shaped leaves that release an odor when crushed and has long been grown in China for strong, jute-like fibre. Its leaves were traditionally eaten in Maldivian mas huni, while its seeds are eaten in China and Kashmir.
edibilityNote: Leaves were traditionally eaten in Maldivian mas huni; seeds are eaten in China and Kashmir.

summary: A perennial wetland herb native to Australia, North America and South America. Its creeping stems form floating or muddy mats, with clustered leaves and bright yellow flowers; where introduced, it can invade and clog waterways.
edibilityNote: It is not commonly ingested and was originally traded as an ornamental.

summary: Aquatic or semiaquatic perennial herb native across North America, South America, Africa, Asia and Europe. It forms sprawling mats with reddish stems that root where they touch the ground. Its greenish-white flowers lack petals, and its fruits are small cube-shaped capsules.
A perennial herb native to Eurasia and North Africa. Its often oblong leaves narrow at the middle like a fiddle, and the upper stem may bend as the fruit develops.

A perennial herb native to much of western North America, particularly parts of California, Arizona and Nevada, willow dock is extremely variable and divided into many varieties of uncertain identity. It usually grows in wet but unflooded places and has flower clusters spaced along its stem.

A perennial flowering aquatic plant native across most of Europe and Asia, and regarded as native in northern and central Africa and Australia. It grows in shallow fresh water or mud, with numerous small white or pale-purple flowers that open in the afternoon. Its starchy rootstocks can be eaten after boiling or soaking to remove bitterness, and aquatic plants should be cooked to kill parasites.
edibilityNote: Starchy rootstocks are eaten after boiling or soaking to remove bitterness; cooking is advised to kill parasites.

summary: A small sedge native to many regions across Australasia, Eurasia, Africa and the Americas, slender club-rush grows on boggy ground and around ponds. It occurs in freshwater wetlands, salt marshes, dune slacks and other brackish environments.

A small annual rush native to Europe, parts of western and central Asia, and parts of northern, eastern, west-central and southern Africa. Its threadlike stems carry clustered flowers with pointed, leaflike bracts often longer than the flower cluster, and it grows in seasonally moist places.

summary: Flowering plant occurring throughout the northern Northern Hemisphere, especially in marshes and other damp habitats. It may be annual or perennial, with fleshy leaves and a dense flower spike resembling sea plantain.

A perennial vegetable of unstated native origin, it produces young shoots harvested in spring from the second or third year. The shoots are prized in English, German and French cooking, while white asparagus is grown by keeping young shoots from light.
edibilityNote: Young shoots are eaten, especially in English, German and French cooking; white shoots are cultivated without light.

summary: A winter annual grass native to eastern and Mediterranean Europe and western Asia. Its rigid late-spring flower spikes bear long, stiff awns, and whole spikelets fall at maturity and spread by animals, wind or water.
A coarse winter annual or biennial grass native to most of South America. It has hairy leaf sheaths and flat, pointed spikelets that may stand erect or droop.

A wild grass native to tropical Asia, barnyardgrass has large, often purplish, millet-like seed heads crowded with seeds, and one plant can produce up to 40,000 seeds annually. Grain from some varieties is eaten during scarcity, while young shoots are eaten as a vegetable.
edibilityNote: Grain from some varieties is eaten during scarcity; in Haryana, seeds are mixed with rice for fasting-day pudding. Young shoots are eaten as a vegetable.

summary: Perennial grass native to most of Europe, Asia, the Arctic and northwestern Africa. Its creeping rhizomes spread rapidly across grassland, producing flat hairy leaves and upright flower spikes.

A perennial grass occurring wild mainly in northern North America and adjacent northeastern Siberia. Its dense, nodding greenish or purplish seed heads bear barbed bristles that readily attach to animals and can seriously injure grazing livestock when dry.
edibilityNote: Kawaiisu people pounded and ate the seeds dry.

summary: Tufted annual grass native to Europe, Asia and northern Africa, and widely naturalised elsewhere. It has green flowers and curved growth reflected in several of its common names.

A perennial bunch grass native to Brazil and Argentina. It forms dense, stiff clumps and spreads by rhizomes, becoming invasive in some introduced areas. Its flower heads have branches neatly lined with beadlike pairs of green to purple spikelets.

Perennial grass whose native range is uncertain, though it probably includes parts of the tropical Americas. It forms clumps, spreads through underground and creeping stems, and usually bears flower clusters on two branches.

A tropical grass native to the highland regions of East Africa, it has very short flowering stems hidden among its leaves. Its rhizomes and creeping stems rapidly form dense mats, helping it spread aggressively and suppress other plants.
A grass native to Africa, Asia and Europe, awned canary-grass has unusually distinctive spikelets. Each spikelet covering bears a hook.

A perennial grass native to virtually all of Europe, North Asia and the mountains of Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia. Its dark blue-green leaves have boat-shaped tips, while creeping underground stems help it form close mats.
An annual grass native to the Mediterranean Basin. Its plume-like flower head is packed with V-shaped spikelets bearing long bristles; elsewhere it occurs as an introduced plant in moist habitats.

A perennial wetland herb native across most of Eurasia and locally in northwestern Africa, narrow-leaved cattail grows in fresh or brackish water. Its slender leaves overtop the flowering stem, whose upper male and lower female sections are separated by a conspicuous bare gap; the female section matures into a rusty-brown, sausage-shaped spike.
edibilityNote: Depending on season, edible parts include dormant root and leaf-base sprouts, stalk cores, green flower spikes, ripe pollen and starchy roots; prepare like broadleaf cattail.

summary: Annual flowering herb native to the Americas and introduced elsewhere as a common weed. It grows from a taproot and bears small, generally white flowers; plants described as xalapensis are glandular-hairy, while those described as peregrina are hairless.

A strongly scented herbaceous perennial native to North Africa and temperate Eurasia. It has silvery-green stems and grey-green leaves covered with silky white hairs. Pale yellow flowers form drooping round heads from early summer to early autumn.
edibilityNote: Used to flavour absinthe and other alcoholic drinks, and historically as a bitter spice in Danish and English beer.

summary: A mound-forming flowering plant native to Madeira. This evergreen biennial or triennial has deeply divided, fern-like leaves and large summer displays of pink flowers on hairy red stems.

A dense, suckering evergreen shrub or small tree native to the Iberian Peninsula and the Caucasus region. It bears violet-purple flowers, often marked with small greenish-yellow spots or streaks. Honey produced with its pollen can be poisonous to humans if consumed in sufficient quantities.
edibilityNote: Honey produced with its pollen can cause severe poisoning when consumed in sufficient quantities.

summary: A flowering shrub native to the tropical and subtropical Americas, though its exact origin is unknown because of widespread cultivation. It has showy clusters of yellow, orange or red flowers, and its immature seeds are reported edible although Caesalpinia seeds are generally poisonous.
edibilityNote: Immature seeds of this species are edible, although Caesalpinia seeds are generally described as poisonous.

summary: A tree endemic to New Zealand’s Kermadec Islands. It is usually multitrunked, bears scarlet, crimson or pink flowers, and is the dominant tree on Raoul Island.

Rhizomatous herbaceous perennial native to cold Northern Hemisphere regions across parts of Europe, northern Asia and North America. It grows in ponds and swamps, with nearly heart-shaped leaves, yellow-green flower spikes and clusters of red berries; the fresh plant is very poisonous, but its rhizomes are edible after boiling or drying.
edibilityNote: The fresh plant is very poisonous, but its rhizomes are edible after boiling or drying.

summary: An aquatic perennial native to Eurasia, flowering-rush grows along the margins of still or slowly moving water. It has long, pointed, twisted leaves and pink flowers. In parts of Russia, its rhizomes are used as food.
edibilityNote: In parts of Russia, the rhizomes are used as food.

summary: A submerged aquatic plant native to Europe and northwestern Asia, with rosettes of serrated leaves and white summer flowers. It floats at the surface in summer, sinks in autumn and rises again in spring; in Britain, naturally occurring plants are female and reproduce mainly through offsets rather than seed.

A compact evergreen flowering perennial found wild around coastal areas of the Northern Hemisphere. It forms low clumps with long stems carrying globes of usually bright pink flowers and tolerates dry, sandy and salty habitats.

summary: A slender herbaceous perennial native to Europe, primarily the Alps and locally England. It has tough, unbranched stems, narrow spirally arranged leaves and five-petalled blue flowers that fall if the stems break.

A deciduous shrub native to western North America, occurring from Oregon to southern California and not known east of the Cascade and Sierra Nevada ranges. Its flowers vary from white to pink and often carry a yellow blotch; it usually grows in wetlands without having submerged roots.

A perennial evergreen native to central North America, Great Plains yucca forms colonies of narrow-leaved rosettes with drooping white or pale-green flowers. Zuni people traditionally boil its seed pods for food, and young flower stalks and unripe fruits can also be cooked and eaten.
edibilityNote: Zuni people traditionally boil the seed pods; young flower stalks and unripe fruits can also be cooked and eaten.

summary: Annual herb native to southern Europe and the Mediterranean Basin. It has clustered flowers enclosed by broad, claw-tipped bracts, with bright pink, magenta or lavender petals marked by darker veins.
A tree native to the Indian subcontinent and Myanmar, lebbeck has very fragrant white flowers and pods containing several seeds. The seeds rattle inside the pods.

Woody shrub native to chaparral and mixed forests in California’s foothills and mountains and some Arizona mountains. It bears spikes of yellow flowers with prominent stamens and shiny, spherical red fruits. The bitter fruits are edible.
edibilityNote: The fruits are bitter but edible.

summary: A pantropical creeping vine found on sandy tropical shores of the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans. It sends long runners across upper beaches and dunes, bearing two-lobed leaves and pink flowers with dark centres. Its saltwater-resistant floating seeds enable ocean dispersal.

A perennial coastal vine whose native origin is not stated, occurring in temperate regions worldwide. It grows in beach sand and has trailing fleshy stems, kidney-shaped leaves and morning-glory-like flowers ranging from delicate pink to vivid lavender.

A perennial flowering herb native to mountainous southern Europe and northwestern Africa. It grows in rock crevices, usually on limestone cliffs, and bears loose flower clusters and dark, crested seeds.

Evergreen perennial flowering plant whose typical subspecies is native to central and north-western Europe, from the British Isles to Austria; another subspecies occurs from Hungary to the Balkans. It has bright oval green leaves and typically golden-yellow flowers, though some plants have blue, purple or blotched blooms.
A small annual herb native to North America. It has woolly, narrow leaves, peg-shaped flower heads in terminal clusters and windborne seeds.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira, Hedypnois cretica is introduced in the Azores.

A dandelion-like herb native to Europe and North Africa, with a ground-level rosette of leaves. Leafless stalks each carry a single yellow flower head; fruits near the centre of the head are rough, while those at the edge are smooth.

An annual mustard-family plant native to temperate North Africa, western Asia and Europe. It grows in beach sand, with fleshy, often purple-tinted leaves and corky segmented fruits that float. The leaves are edible, preferably cooked and not in large quantities.
edibilityNote: Leaves are edible, preferably cooked and not eaten in large quantities.

summary: An annual or biennial herb of uncertain origin, though often cited as native to South America. Its inconspicuous flowers may lack petals, while its paired, rounded fruits contain orange or reddish-brown seeds; the edible leaves have a salty cress or mustard flavour.
edibilityNote: The leaves are edible and have a salty cress or mustard flavour.

summary: A submerged, free-floating aquatic flowering plant native to every continent except Antarctica. It forms bushy masses of brittle, spiny-toothed leaves, which fork only once or twice and help distinguish it from soft coontail.

An annual wild pea native to Europe, North Africa and much of Asia, hairy vetchling has winged stems and paired leaflets ending in coiled, branching tendrils. Its pink, blue or two-coloured flowers are followed by hairy pods, while the rest of the plant is generally hairless.
Herbaceous perennial flowering vine native to Europe. It has winged, hairless stems with branched tendrils and unscented purplish-pink flowers that fade with age.
edibilityNote: The seeds are poisonous.

summary: Evergreen flowering shrub indigenous to coastal California, though its exact native range is uncertain and may extend from Point Reyes south to San Luis Obispo County. It bears fragrant, pea-like flowers, usually soft yellow but sometimes lilac or purple. Outside its native range it has escaped cultivation and become invasive in many regions.
A sprawling flowering plant native to the Mediterranean basin. It usually has three-part leaves marked with spots, pale-yellow spring and summer flowers, and unusually coiled, sharply spiny pods.
edibilityNote: The plant is stated to be edible to humans, but no parts or preparation are specified.

summary: Annual clover native to Eurasia and North Africa. Its mostly hairless stems range from low-spreading to upright, and its leaf axils carry dense clusters of pink flowers with outward-bending, triangular sepal tips.

An annual herb with no native origin specified in the supplied information, Trifolium tomentosum occurs in Mediterranean and tropical climates and southern Africa. Its fruiting flower cup becomes rounded and hairy while the rest of the plant is hairless. It has three toothed leaflets and heads of pink flowers.

summary: Annual herb native to the Mediterranean basin, parts of western Asia, Macaronesia, Great Britain, Crimea, Chad and Socotra. It is self-supporting and has simple, broad leaves.

An annual or biennial herb found in the Middle East, bull mallow has a hairy, upright stem. Its pinkish to light purple flowers grow where the leaves meet the stem, followed by disc-shaped, segmented fruit. The leaves and stems are eaten, often chopped and fried with olive oil, onions and spices, and historically fed besieged Jewish settlers during the 1948 Battle for Jerusalem.
edibilityNote: Leaves and stems are eaten, including fried as garnish or cooked like spinach; they fed besieged Jewish settlers in Jerusalem in 1948.

summary: An annual flowering herb native to western North America, occurring in coastal hills and mountains from British Columbia to California's San Francisco Bay Area. Its showy, four-petalled flowers range from pink to pale purple and bloom from late spring into early summer.

A tuft-forming annual grass native to Europe, where it grows in dry sandy ground, rocky outcrops and heath grassland. Its narrow basal leaves accompany tightly clustered, purple-tinged green flower spikes, which appear from April to June.

A perennial grass widespread across much of the Northern Hemisphere, with no specific native origin stated. Its narrow, needle-like bright green leaves form tufts or spreading growth, and it is widely planted as shade-tolerant turf or groundcover.

A clump-forming annual grass native to the Mediterranean Basin and nearby regions, from Madeira and the Canary Islands to Crimea and Saudi Arabia. Its short oval flowerheads change from green to buff as they ripen and are valued ornamentally.

A perennial aquatic plant reported across much of the world, though the extent of that distribution is debated; it generally grows in brackish or saline coastal waters. Its thin submerged leaves can form dense layers, while its tiny petal-less flowers produce fruit on a long stalk that often coils but is rarely seen.

summary: An aquatic annual or perennial herb found worldwide, especially in coastal brackish wetlands. It is a salt-tolerant freshwater plant with thread-thin, grasslike growth and tiny flowers whose pollen may float away on bubbles.

A non-woody perennial native to temperate Asia, Europe, northern Africa and northern North America, it grows in wet habitats. Its creeping stem roots at the joints before rising through surrounding vegetation, bearing very narrow pointed leaves and sparse spikes of pale flowers.
A perennial plant whose native origin is not specified in the supplied information. Moth larvae of Plusia festucae feed on it.

An annual flowering plant with no stated native origin, sand catchfly is widespread in dunes and sandy soils across Europe and western Asia. Its bright pink petals and prominent parallel veins around each flower make it readily recognizable.

A deciduous shrub native to eastern North America. Its red fruits often remain on bare branches into winter, but its seeds, leaves, bark and berries can cause nausea and low blood pressure if swallowed.
edibilityNote: Seeds, leaves, bark and berries can cause nausea and low blood pressure if ingested.

summary: A perennial aquatic or semi-aquatic herb native to Canada, the United States and northern Mexico, it grows in shallow water or mud. Long-stalked leaves form a clump around a flowering stem bearing white or pink-tinged flowers.

A herbaceous perennial native to the British Isles, much of the Mediterranean region, the Caucasus, Canary Islands, Madeira and northern Africa. Its white spring flowers give way to showy red fruit, and its flower structure produces heat. In Croatia, corms were eaten during famines, though the leaves, fruits and rhizomes are poisonous and tuber ingestion may be fatal.
edibilityNote: Corms were eaten in Croatia during famines; leaves, fruits and rhizomes are poisonous, and tuber ingestion may be fatal.

summary: A deciduous tree or multi-stemmed bush native to western Eurasia, the European wild apple has a densely branched crown and often spiny branches. Its small fruits ripen in autumn, and frequent hybridisation with cultivated apples can make identification difficult.

A flowering plant of the rose family known from California, Argentina and Chile, Argentinian biddy-biddy occurs on Californian roadsides, dunes, rocky slopes and coastal grasslands. The California population is sometimes treated as a separate species or variety, and that variety is described as confined to coastal scrub and open rocky slopes.

A deciduous shrub native to Japan, Japanese quince has thorny, spreading branches and vivid red, white, pink or multicoloured flowers. Its golden-yellow, apple-shaped fruit is edible but hard and astringent unless bletted or cooked, and is occasionally made into jam, jelly or pies.
edibilityNote: The fruit is edible after bletting or cooking and occasionally used in jam, jelly and pies; kernels contain small amounts of poison.

summary: A perennial blackberry native to Armenia and northwestern Iran, it grows vigorously into dense tangles of arching, prickly stems and is invasive elsewhere. Its large fruit is edible and sweet when ripe.
edibilityNote: The large fruit is edible and sweet when ripe; immature fruit is hard, red and much sourer.

summary: A woodland flowering plant native across most of Europe, Eastern Turkey and the Caucasus, cuckoo-pint has arrow-shaped leaves and a hooded flower spike that smells of faeces and traps insects. Its autumn berries are extremely poisonous, but the root is edible when thoroughly roasted, and leaves are eaten in parts of Turkey and by Roma in Sliven only after extensive processing.
edibilityNote: The root is edible when well roasted; leaves are eaten after prolonged boiling with yogurt or after drying and boiling with several changes of water.

summary: An annual herb native to South Africa’s Cape Province, it has hairy stems and white-and-yellow flowers. In Western Australia, it grows in sandy soils, lawns and along road verges, flowering from July to October.

A herbaceous perennial native to temperate Europe and Asia, northern Africa and eastern Australia. It forms extensive colonies of square, reddish-purple stems topped with tightly clustered reddish-purple flowers.

A non-vascular land plant called a liverwort, snakewort has a broad Holarctic distribution. It grows in wet or moist, shaded places, often on rocks or thin soil, and tolerates drying and reduced shade better than Conocephalum conicum.
A highly fragrant daffodil native to central and southern Europe. Its flowers have pure-white outer parts and a short pale-yellow cup with a distinct red edge; the plant is poisonous when eaten.
edibilityNote: All narcissi are poisonous when eaten; poet's daffodil is especially dangerous, acting as a strong emetic and irritant.

summary: Tropical and subtropical vine native from the tropical and subtropical Old World to the South Pacific. Its hollow, oblong fruit has a distinctive warty exterior and bitter flesh. Green or early-yellow fruit is generally cooked, while young shoots and leaves are eaten as greens; ripe fruit and mature seeds are toxic.
edibilityNote: Green or early-yellow fruit is cooked; young shoots and leaves are greens. Sweet red ripe pith is eaten raw, but ripe fruit and mature seeds are toxic.

summary: An erect annual herb, it may be native to Australia, the Americas, or both. It has dark green leaves, pale yellow five-sided flowers and yellow-orange fruits enclosed in balloon-like husks. Ripe fruits are eaten raw and the fruit may also be cooked or made into jam, but unripe raw fruits and all other parts are poisonous.
edibilityNote: Ripe fruits are traditionally eaten raw by Toba-Pilagá people; fruit may also be cooked or made into jam. Unripe raw fruits and other parts are poisonous.

summary: A frost-sensitive annual herb native to Mexico. Its small, round green or purple fruit is enclosed in a papery husk that browns and splits as the fruit ripens. The fruit is widely eaten in Latin American green sauces and Mexican dishes, but other plant parts should not be used as food because they contain toxins.
edibilityNote: The fruit is used in green sauces, salads and garnishes; other plant parts should not be eaten because they contain toxins.

summary: A cultivated cereal grass first domesticated in China’s Yangtze River basin 13,500 to 8,200 years ago. Its major forms include sticky, short-grained japonica and nonsticky, long-grained indica, while the grain may be white, brown, black or red.
edibilityNote: Cultivated as a cereal, with grain occurring in several colors.

summary: A perennial herb native to western Europe, the British Isles and Norway, pignut grows in hedgerows, woods and fields. Its chestnut-like underground part is sometimes eaten as a wild or cultivated root vegetable, and cultivation produces larger tubers.
edibilityNote: The chestnut-like underground part is eaten as a wild or cultivated root vegetable; cultivation produces larger tubers.

summary: Evergreen cherry shrub or small to medium-sized tree native to regions bordering the Black Sea in southwestern Asia and southeastern Europe. It has dark green, leathery, shiny leaves that may smell of almonds when crushed, creamy-white sweet-smelling flowers, and small cherries that turn black when ripe in early autumn.
edibilityNote: The astringent fruits are edible, but bitter fruits should not be eaten; seeds and leaves contain more hydrogen cyanide and should never be eaten.

summary: A colonising perennial herb native to Europe and a broad Asian range extending from the Caucasus and Siberia to Nepal and Japan. Its arching stems carry alternate leaves and scented white tubular flowers with green tips that hang beneath them in spring.
edibilityNote: Young shoots may be boiled like asparagus, and the root is used for tea in Korea; stems, leaves and berries may be toxic in large quantities.

summary: An annual wildflower with a subspecies native to Europe and western Asia, yellow rattle has dry fruits whose loose ripe seeds audibly rattle. Its roots can opportunistically draw nutrients from neighbouring plants, especially grasses and legumes.

A bulbous perennial herb native across the Mediterranean from Portugal to the Levant. It bears rounded clusters of up to 25 white flowers with yellow anthers and has become naturalized in many other regions.

A semi-evergreen flowering perennial native to southwestern and south-central Europe. Its hairy, branching stems trail or rise slightly, bearing mainly red or pink flowers with blue anthers from May to August in the Northern Hemisphere.

Prostrate perennial flowering plant native to Eurasia and Africa. It has dark green, heart-shaped leaves and produces several violet flowers in May and June, often along woodland edges, grassland and shady hedge banks.

A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, it grows near streams in wet woods. In mainland Portugal, a 2020 assessment recorded it only in the Estrela and Montesinho mountains and classified it as Vulnerable.

summary: A perennial herb native to southern Africa. It grows from rhizomes and bulbs, sometimes forms small bulblets above ground, and bears three-part leaves and solitary white-to-light-pink flowers.

Tall flowering shrub or tree native to coastal and tableland areas of New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory. It has dark green, finely divided leaves, golden spherical flower heads and thin, leathery pods. The flowers are eaten in fritters, while edible trunk gum can substitute for gum arabic in fruit jelly.
edibilityNote: Flowers are used in fritters; edible trunk gum can substitute for gum arabic, including in fruit jelly.

summary: An annual herb native to southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa. Its winged stem climbs using coiled tendrils, and it bears red pea flowers followed by smooth pods that split open.

A perennial flowering plant native to Europe. Its three-part leaves are unmarked, while pale pink or whitish flower heads rise on stalks from the leaf joints. It commonly grows in fields and along roadsides.

Bulbous perennial native to Cape Province in South Africa, where it grows among rocks. Its showy, fragrant pink flowers appear on leafless stems in late summer or autumn, before the narrow leaves. All parts are toxic and can cause vomiting and diarrhoea in humans.
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic; ingestion can cause vomiting and diarrhoea in humans.

summary: Perennial herb native to Mexico and parts of Central and South America. It grows from small bulbs, spreads by runners and has stemless leaves with three broad, heart-shaped leaflets; its five-petalled flowers are pink, though some varieties have white flowers.

An evergreen shrub native to the Mediterranean Basin. Its greyish, downy leaves sit below pink-to-purple flower spikes crowned with much larger bright lavender-purple sterile bracts. It blooms in spring and early summer, from March in its native habitat depending on the climate.

An annual or biennial herb native to Europe and North Africa, it has sharp bristles with swollen, blister-like bases on its leaves and stems. Its yellow flowerheads have a distinctive outer row of large bracts.
edibilityNote: Leaves were formerly eaten as a pot herb; some modern foragers use the flowers to flavour vinegar.

summary: An annual or biennial herb native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, it has low, spreading stems and sharp, needle-like leaves. Its small, mostly self-pollinated flowers lack petals, and its seeds may germinate in autumn or spring under several different life cycles.
A perennial flowering herb native to Eurasia, lesser stitchwort has weak, four-angled stems and narrow leaves. Each white petal is so deeply divided that it appears to be two petals.

A perennial bulbous herb native to South America, large-flowered pink-sorrel now grows in temperate and tropical regions worldwide except Antarctica. In Europe, plants are sterile and reproduce only through bulbs; its leaves have a zesty, lemony flavour.
edibilityNote: Flowers, leaves and roots are edible, but consumption in large amounts is discouraged because the plant contains oxalic acid.

summary: A deciduous tree native to western Eurasia, wild cherry has white spring flowers and ripe red to dark-purple fruit. The ripe fruit has been eaten by people for thousands of years, while every other part is slightly toxic.
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit has been human food for millennia; all other plant parts are slightly toxic and contain cyanogenic glycosides.

summary: A parasitic plant native mainly to central and northern Europe and parts of Asia, ivy broomrape lacks chlorophyll and depends completely on ivy. Its brown, purple or sometimes yellow stems bear cream flowers with reddish-purple veins and a pointed top of unopened flowers.
edibilityNote: Dioscorides wrote that the plant could be eaten raw or cooked like asparagus.

summary: An aquatic flowering plant native to North Africa, Europe, temperate Asia and Jammu and Kashmir in tropical Asia. Its round dark-green leaves and white flowers float on water; the daytime summer flowers open cup-shaped and become star-shaped over time.
edibilityNote: In north-eastern India, young leaves and flower stalks are eaten as vegetables, while rhizomes are boiled and eaten.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to most of Europe, the Maghreb, Levant and Caucasus, grass vetchling lacks true leaves, leaflets and tendrils. Its flattened leaf stalks resemble pointed grass blades, while small crimson flowers give way to long pods that become cylindrical as the peas develop.

A rhizomatous perennial flowering plant native to Western Europe. Its heart-shaped leaves have transparent dots, while its rich yellow flowers have petals that are red underneath and dotted along the margins.

A perennial herb found across Europe, western Siberia, Asia Minor, the Caucasus and North Africa, dropwort favours dry, lime-rich pasture. It has fern-like leaves and clusters of creamy white flowers; mature crushed leaves smell of wintergreen. Its tuberous roots and young leaves can be eaten raw or cooked and taste bittersweet.
edibilityNote: Tuberous roots and young leaves can be eaten raw as salad or cooked as a vegetable; their taste is bittersweet.

summary: A member of the carrot family native to western Europe, it bears frilly leaves and a small rounded taproot. The root, once used as a vegetable in parts of western Europe, is edible raw or cooked, while the leaves can serve as an herb or garnish.
edibilityNote: The taproot is edible raw or cooked and was formerly a western European root vegetable; leaves can be used as an herb or garnish.

summary: An annual flowering herb native to continental Europe. It has small blue tubular flowers and coarse hairs, while its unusually bristly, warty-looking leaves help distinguish it from similar species.

An ornamental flowering plant of unstated native origin, hollyhock reached Europe from southwestern China by the 15th century, possibly earlier. It has large, heart-shaped leaves and large flowers, and may grow as an annual, biennial or short-lived perennial while frequently self-sowing.

A flowering plant native to eastern and central North America. Usually living for two years, it forms a low leaf rosette first, then sends up a flowering stem whose yellow blooms open quickly each evening and last until the following noon. Most parts are edible: roots and leaves may be raw or cooked, while young stems should be peeled before eating raw or fried.
edibilityNote: Indigenous North Americans historically used it as food; roots and leaves are eaten raw or cooked, while young stems are peeled before eating raw or fried.

summary: A generally biennial herb with no natural native range supplied, this evening primrose arose as a garden hybrid in Europe. Its showy flower spikes have long red sepals and bright yellow petals that fade through orange to red. Cultivation has helped it spread and become naturalized in many countries.

Perennial herb native to Eurasia, sulphur cinquefoil grows in tufts from a woody taproot and has upright, densely hairy, branching stems. It usually bears pale yellow flowers with five broad, shallowly notched petals from June to August.
A flowering sedge, cyperus sedge grows in marshes, swamps and along ponds, rivers and canals. It bears one male flower spike and several hanging female spikes among bright yellow-green leaves.

A perennial herb native to western North America, it grows from a layered bulb and bears grass-like leaves and blue, star-shaped flowers. Its bulbs are eaten after roasting or boiling, but are easily confused with toxic death-camas bulbs.
edibilityNote: Bulbs are roasted, boiled or made into flour; they are difficult to distinguish from poisonous death-camas bulbs.

summary: A deciduous shrub native to western North America. It becomes covered in white blossoms with a strong orange-and-pineapple scent, and Native American tribes use the flowers to prepare teas.
edibilityNote: Native American tribes use the flowers to prepare teas.

summary: A milky-sapped perennial native to western North America. It bears dense clusters of pale pink to pinkish-purple, star-shaped flowers and rough pods filled with silky-haired seeds. Young leaves and seed pods can be boiled and eaten, but care is needed to distinguish it from highly toxic related species.
edibilityNote: Young leaves and seed pods can be boiled and eaten; careful identification is needed because related milkweeds may be highly toxic.

summary: An annual flowering garden plant native to southern Europe, North Africa and southwest Asia, love-in-a-mist has flowers nestled among lacy bracts. Its flowers are usually blue but may be white, pink or pale purple, followed by large, inflated seed capsules that turn brown in late summer.

A parasitic plant native to Europe, greater dodder grows on many herbaceous plants and is a notable parasite of lucerne. Its long, thin stems are yellowish or reddish, bearing compact clusters of pink flowers.

Yellow loosestrife is a perennial flowering plant native to Eurasia, including Ireland, and North Africa. It has an upright, downy form, conspicuous yellow flower clusters and leaves spotted with translucent orange glands.
A flowering plant, dense-flowered mullein occurs in Madeira, where it is introduced.

A hardy annual leaf vegetable native to Asia and Europe. Its red, white or green varieties have thin, slightly acidic leaves with a salty, spinach-like taste. The leaves are eaten raw in salads or cooked and were once used to colour pasta in Italy.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw in salads or cooked; green leaves were formerly used to colour pasta in Italy.

summary: A low evergreen shrub native to northeastern North America, eastern teaberry has wintergreen-scented leaves and red fruits. Its mildly sweet fruits are edible, while dried leaves and branches are infused as herbal tea; significant essential oil from the leaves requires at least three days of fermentation.
edibilityNote: Fruits are eaten; dried leaves and branches make tea. Leaves require at least three days’ fermentation to yield significant essential oil.

summary: A root-hemiparasitic plant native to parts of the eastern and midwestern United States and adjacent Canada. It attaches to oak roots and is recognized by its fern-like lobed leaves and tubular yellow flowers.
A very small annual herb native to continental Europe. It has alternate leaves and glandular hairs, with flowers ranging from pale purple to white and appearing in June and July.

A usually biennial wildflower native to northern Eurasia, ragwort can behave as a perennial under repeated grazing or mowing. It has unpleasant-smelling leaves and dense clusters of bright yellow flowers, blooming from June to November in the Northern Hemisphere.
An annual herb endemic to California. Its densely hairy, glandular stems carry branching clusters of sticky flower heads, each with resin glands and golden-yellow outer florets.

Perennial aquatic flowering herb with a circumboreal range across northern Eurasia and North America. Its straplike leaves may float or stand above shallow water, and its spherical female fruiting heads grow below the male flower heads.

An annual or perennial herb native to eastern Canada and the United States. It has branching stems, gland-dotted leaves and tiny golden-yellow, star-shaped flowers that appear from July to September. It grows in ditches, marshes, shorelines and sometimes moist woods and fields.

Annual nightshade native to the United States and northern and central Mexico, it forms a tumbleweed and has abundant spines on its stems and leaves. Its yellow flowers contain two unequal sets of anthers, and each berry is enclosed by a prickly covering.

A perennial climbing vine native primarily to subtropical and temperate East Asia, kudzu has tuberous, starch-rich roots and stems that root on contact with soil. Its starchy root has been eaten in China since before 540 CE and is still made into starch, flour, noodles and Japanese sweets.
edibilityNote: The starchy root has been eaten in China since before 540 CE and is processed into starch, flour, noodles and Japanese sweets.

summary: Annual flowering plant, sometimes biennial or perennial, native to eastern and central North America. Its coarse-haired leaves and stems bear yellow, daisy-like flowers with prominent dark, dome-shaped centres in late summer and early autumn.

Perennial vine native to the southeastern United States, especially the Cumberland and Blue Ridge Mountains. Its large, heart-shaped leaves form dense cover, while yellowish-green flowers with brownish-purple lobes resemble smoking pipes.

A tropical tree native to Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and northern South America. Its trunk and large branches are often crowded with thorns, and it flowers while briefly leafless. The pods contain seeds surrounded by buoyant, cotton-like fibre traditionally used as stuffing and insulation.

A tropical fruit plant native to the tropical Americas, probably southern Mexico and adjacent Central America. Its usually single trunk bears large, deeply lobed leaves near the top, while hard green berries mature into yellow fruit with soft orange flesh. Papayas are eaten fresh, in salads and juices; before ripening, the skin’s milky latex should be removed because it harms mucous membranes.
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten fresh, in salads and juices; milky latex from unripe skin should be removed before consumption.

summary: A large tropical tree of uncertain native origin because people have spread it widely. Its branches grow in distinctive tiers, and its corky fruit can travel by water. The slightly acidic fruit is edible; ripe seeds may be eaten raw or cooked but are small and difficult to extract.
edibilityNote: The slightly acidic fruit is edible; ripe seeds can be eaten raw or cooked but are small and difficult to extract.

summary: A perennial flowering tree native from the southwestern United States and northern Mexico south to the Galápagos Islands and northern Argentina. Its tiny leaflets fall in dry weather, leaving green stalks and branches to photosynthesize, while sharp spines and fragrant yellow-orange flowers make it distinctive.

A large, fast-growing tree native to Central America and Mexico, the avocado has glossy leaves and pear-shaped fruit with creamy, fatty, pale green or yellow flesh. Wild fruits are small, while cultivated varieties can be much larger; the flesh surrounding the large seed is edible.
edibilityNote: The edible part is the soft, greenish-yellow flesh surrounding the large seed; the fruit is nutritious for humans.

summary: A tree native to the Neotropics, it grows naturally in well-drained tropical and subtropical forests from Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean to much of South America. Its aromatic, rot-resistant wood is widely used for storage furniture, veneer and musical instruments.

Deciduous flowering tree native to Madagascar. It is remembered for fern-like bright-green leaves and a summer display of large scarlet or orange-red flowers, usually with a larger upright petal spotted yellow and white. It is endangered in the wild but widely cultivated elsewhere.

Evergreen shrub or small tree native to South America, specifically Peru, common guava bears edible fruit that may be eaten raw or cooked. Cultivars have white, pink, or red flesh, and a few have red rather than green or yellow skin.
edibilityNote: The fruit can be eaten raw or cooked.

summary: Evergreen coastal tree native across the tropical Old World and Oceania, with a separate subspecies native to tropical America; its status in Hawaii is uncertain. Its yellow flowers turn orange and then red during the day, and its young leafy shoots may be eaten as vegetables.
edibilityNote: Young leafy shoots may be eaten as vegetables; leaves are also used as cooking trays and in tempeh fermentation.

summary: Shrub native to tropical eastern Africa, specifically Kenya, Tanzania and Mozambique. Its distinctive red or pink flowers have frilly, finely divided petals.

A large deciduous tree native to the tropical monsoon forests of Southeast Asia, specifically India, Myanmar, Thailand and Laos. Its pale, durable, relatively light wood is especially valued for shipbuilding, while the tree has large rounded leaves and small clustered flowers.

Evergreen flowering tree native to the western Pacific, Australia, New Guinea, Southeast Asia and India. Its foliage consists of slender, drooping branchlets bearing tiny scale-like leaves, and its woody fruit resembles a conifer cone although the tree is not a conifer.
A flowering plant reported as native to the tropical Americas and now introduced across most continents. It has spines at its nodes and green, petal-free flowers arranged in spikes.
edibilityNote: The plant is eaten in Africa and several Asian cuisines; its leaves are dietary in the Maldives, and it is braised or added to porridge in Brazil.

summary: An evergreen subshrub or herbaceous perennial native and endemic to Madagascar, Madagascar periwinkle has glossy green leaves in opposite pairs, each with a pale central vein. Its flowers range from white with yellow or red centres to dark pink, and all parts are poisonous if eaten.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous; eating them can cause stomach cramps, heart complications, low blood pressure, paralysis and death.

summary: An erect succulent shrub native to arid and subtropical South Asia, mainly the Indian Subcontinent. Its ridged, angular branches bear short spines and small leaves that fall quickly. Every part contains poisonous, irritating milky latex.

A flowering plant native to Bolivia, Brazil, French Guiana, Guyana, Suriname and Venezuela, golden trumpet is widely naturalised elsewhere in the tropics. It is cultivated as a houseplant and needs bright light, abundant moisture and organic-rich soil during growth.

A climbing plant of unspecified native origin, lesser balloon vine is widely distributed across tropical and subtropical Africa, Australia, South Asia and North America. It has balloon-like capsules that turn brown when ripe and almost black seeds marked with a pale heart-shaped spot.
edibilityNote: The green parts are eaten as vegetables.

summary: A woody flowering vine or shrub native to Brazil, Bolivia, Peru and Chubut Province in Argentina. Its thorny, hairy stems bear heart-shaped leaves, while small white flowers are surrounded by brightly coloured bracts.

Woody perennial herb or small shrub native to coastal sage and chaparral from Southern California into Baja California. It ranges from a low vine to a stout woody climber, with broad triangular leaves and white, pale pink or lavender flowers whose colour often varies with drought or temperature.

A perennial herb native through most of Europe and western Asia, typically growing in damp meadows. Its divided leaves are dark green above and whitish beneath, while its numerous creamy-white summer flowers have a strong sweet scent and are used to flavour drinks, fruit, jams and desserts.
edibilityNote: Flowers flavour stewed fruit, jams and desserts; the aromatic plant also flavours vinegar, wine, beer and Scandinavian mead.

summary: Cactus native to Argentina, particularly the provinces of Salta and Tucumán at lower altitudes. It usually grows singly and produces long, unscented white flowers that open at night.

A tall perennial grass now found worldwide, reed canary grass often forms single-species stands beside lakes and streams or in wet open ground. It spreads underground through thick rhizomes; in many places it invades wetlands and is difficult to eradicate.

A perennial mustard-family plant native to Europe and western to central Asia. It bears white flower clusters and heart-shaped seed pods, while its creeping roots can produce dense, long-lived patches.
Perennial flowering plant native to Europe, with very large oval leaves that may have red stems and slightly wavy edges. Its small greenish flowers turn red as they mature.
edibilityNote: Young leaves are eaten as greens but soon become bitter; dried seeds can be ground into flour.

summary: A shrub or tree native to southeastern Australia. It has bright to pale-yellow cylindrical flower spikes and straight to strongly twisted seed pods, and is considered invasive in Portugal, New Zealand and South Africa.
edibilityNote: Flowers, seeds and pods are used as food; in Tasmania, ripening pods were roasted and the seeds eaten.

summary: A small deciduous tree native to Japan and southern Korea, it has rounded, many-lobed leaves that begin downy and turn bright orange to dark red in autumn. Dark purplish-red flowers hang in clusters as the leaves open in early spring.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native to Korea, Japan, China, eastern Mongolia and far eastern Russia, Japanese maple has sharply pointed, hand-shaped leaves and paired winged fruits. Its seedlings vary notably in leaf size, shape and colour, while cultivated forms range from upright to weeping. The edible leaves are locally pickled for a year, coated with flour, sesame and sugar, then deep-fried as momiji tempura.
edibilityNote: Leaves are edible; for the Minoh dish momiji tempura, they are pickled for a year, coated with flour, sesame and sugar, then deep-fried.

summary: A large coniferous tree native to Northern, Central and Eastern Europe, Norway spruce typically has hanging branchlets and the longest cones of any spruce. Its seed cones mature from green or reddish to brown.
edibilityNote: The tree supplies spruce beer; in Finland, shoot tips are used in syrup, tea, alcohol, smoothies, salt and desserts.

summary: A fast-growing evergreen shrub or small tree endemic to New Zealand. Its lance-shaped, finely serrated leaves have translucent dots, while its white flowers bear purple spots and are followed by bright red fruit. The berries were occasionally eaten traditionally by Māori, but consumption is not recommended because the plant contains the toxin ngaione.
edibilityNote: Berries were occasionally a traditional Māori food, but consumption is not recommended because of the toxin ngaione.

summary: Evergreen conifer native to the Mediterranean region, although its precise natural range is debated. Young trees are bushy, while mature trees develop broad, flat, umbrella-like crowns. Its pine nuts are edible and have been cultivated since prehistoric times.
edibilityNote: Edible pine nuts have been cultivated for at least 6,000 years and traded since early historic times.

summary: A large evergreen conifer native to northwestern North America, grand fir has flattened needles arranged in nearly level rows. Its foliage has a citrus-like scent, and the taller coastal variety grows west of the Cascades while the shorter interior variety grows to the east.

A deciduous shrub or small tree of unspecified native origin, the plum may be somewhat thorny and bears white blossom in early spring. Its fruit has one large stone and usually sweet edible pulp, although some varieties are sour and require cooking with sugar to be palatable.
edibilityNote: The pulp is edible; sour varieties may require cooking with sugar to become palatable, and the stone is discarded.

summary: A fern native to western Europe, pillwort grows on wet mud and silt around lakes, ponds, ditches and marshes, sometimes in shallow water. Its slender, rush-like fronds curl as they unfurl, and populations may disappear from a site before returning years later.
