summary: A medium-sized deciduous tree native to western North America, Oregon ash develops dark gray-brown bark with deep, woven-looking ridges. Its light green leaves turn bright yellow and fall early in autumn. When leafless, it can be recognized by stout, oppositely arranged twigs with woolly hairs.

Annual herb native across most of the world, from Arctic to tropical regions, except South America and southern Africa. It has reddish stems with swollen joints, often dark-blotched leaves, and dense, often nodding spikes of tiny pink flowers. Remains were identified in the intestinal contents of Tollund Man in Denmark.
edibilityNote: Remains were found in Tollund Man’s intestinal contents in Denmark; the plant part and preparation are unspecified.

summary: A tiny floating aquatic plant found widely outside polar and tropical regions. Its simple body carries one dangling root and can form green mats over still water, though it also grows on mud or damp rocks.
A fern native to humid warm-temperate and tropical regions worldwide. It has delicate, divided light-green fronds on black, wiry stems and commonly grows in moist, sheltered, shaded places.

A deciduous vine native to western North America, California wild grape climbs other plants or trails across the ground on twisted woody stems. Its small, often sour purple grapes ripen in autumn and are edible, including for making wine or jelly.
edibilityNote: Small, often sour purple grapes are eaten and can be made into wine or jelly.

summary: A large deciduous tree native at least to southwest and central Asia and southeast Europe, though ancient cultivation obscures its exact natural range. Its fruit has a green husk around a corrugated shell and a rich-flavoured edible nut; cultivated trees usually have thinner shells than wild ones.
edibilityNote: The nuts are eaten fresh or pressed for richly flavoured oil; cultivated forms are commonly selected for larger, thinner-shelled nuts.

summary: A pear species native to central and eastern Europe and western Asia. Most orchard pears grown in Europe, North America and Australia derive from it; the fruit is eaten fresh or cooked and fermented into perry.
edibilityNote: Pears are eaten fresh or cooked in desserts and pies, served with meat, or fermented into perry and distilled into pear brandy.

summary: A small pear tree distributed across southern Iberia and northern Morocco. Within Iberia, its distribution is fragmented and trees are often sparse. It has white, occasionally pink-tinged flowers and fibrous green or brown fruits, which mammals often eat whole and disperse.
edibilityNote: The fruit is described as inedible for people, though the source flags this claim as needing citation.

summary: A deciduous flowering shrub native and endemic to California, California sweetshrub grows along streams and on moist canyon slopes. Its dark red to burgundy flowers appear from late spring to early fall and are pollinated by beetles.

A tall perennial cane native to the Greater Middle East. It forms dense stands in damp places and bears upright, feathery plumes whose seeds are usually absent or rarely fertile; it spreads mainly through tough underground rhizomes. It is widely naturalised and considered invasive in North America and Oceania.

A pine tree native to coastal and inland mountain areas along the Pacific coast of North America, from Oregon to Baja California, sugar pine is the tallest and most massive pine and bears some of the longest cones of any conifer. Indigenous peoples ate its seeds raw or roasted, ground them into flour or paste, ate the inner bark, and consumed small amounts of sweet resin or chewed it as gum.
edibilityNote: Indigenous peoples ate seeds raw, roasted, as flour or paste, ate inner bark, and consumed small amounts of resin or chewed it as gum.

summary: A pine tree ranging from southern Oregon to Baja California, especially northern California and the Oregon–California border. Its twisted yellow-green needles grow in threes, while resin-sealed cones cluster on branches and sometimes the trunk; fire melts the resin and releases seeds for regrowth.

Fern native to the Western Pacific rim, from Australia through New Caledonia and Fiji to French Polynesia. It is commonly known as monarch fern, musk fern, maile-scented fern, breadfruit fern or wart fern.

A herbaceous perennial native to the United States, from Connecticut to Missouri and south from Florida to Texas. Its lyre-shaped leaves form a basal rosette, while hairy square stems carry lavender to blue flowers. It can spread readily into lawns and tolerate mowing and foot traffic.

A flowering plant native to Mexico and Texas. It bears large, spiny-edged leaves and flowers only once near the end of its life, producing a tall stalk of yellow blooms before dying while new shoots continue from its base.
edibilityNote: In pre-Columbian Mexico, liquid from a cut pre-flowering stem was fermented into pulque; heated hearts are also used to produce mezcal.

summary: A herbaceous climbing plant native to eastern and southern Africa. It has shiny, flattened, leaf-like stems and hanging white flowers, while radial tubers cluster close to its underground stem.

An evergreen woody climber native to the Canary Islands, using aerial rootlets to cling to trees, cliffs and walls or spreading as ground cover. It has broad, glossy, slightly leathery leaves, greenish flowers and round fruits that turn black when ripe.

Perennial flowering shrub native to Mexico and invasive in farmland and bushland worldwide. It has creamy-white flower clusters and seeds with feathery parachutes carried by wind; stems can also root when they touch soil.

A perennial cactus shrub with a likely wild origin in central Mexico, the Indian fig opuntia has thick, succulent, paddle-shaped stems and white, yellow or red flowers. Its fruits are eaten raw, while its young stems are cooked and eaten as a vegetable.
edibilityNote: Fruits are eaten raw; young stems are cooked as a vegetable called nopalitos.

summary: A shrub or small tree found in chaparral canyons and slopes of Southern California, Arizona and the Baja California peninsula. It is long-lived, with dense evergreen foliage, leathery folded leaves and reddish, hairy, sticky fruit.
edibilityNote: Cahuilla ate fresh, dried or mashed fruits and boiled flower clusters; Kumeyaay cooked, toasted, ground or infused fruits. Seeds are reportedly inedible.

summary: Large evergreen shrub or small tree native to North America, laurel sumac occurs along the Pacific coast of Southern California and Baja California. Its folded, fragrant leaves have bright reddish veins and edges throughout the year. The Chumash made flour from its dried fruit.
edibilityNote: The Chumash historically made flour from the dried fruit.

summary: A tree endemic to Australia, river red gum is strongly associated with inland watercourses and has smooth pale bark and white flowers. Its limbs, and sometimes whole trees, can fall without warning.
A biennial herb native to Great Britain, Italy, France, the Iberian Peninsula, the Canary Islands and Madeira. It grows tall and bears yellow flowers with purple centres.

A small deciduous tree native to southwestern North America, from southern California to Texas and northern Mexico. It has rough, fissured gray-brown bark and noticeably velvety young shoots. Male and female flowers grow on separate trees in small clusters during early spring.

A perennial grass native to southern Africa and Yemen, it grows in many habitats, including shade. It flowers and sets seed throughout the year, and its seeds can produce new plants within a few weeks; it is invasive in several regions.

A perennial grass native to southern Europe, Macaronesia, North and East Africa, western and central Asia, India, Yunnan and Vietnam. It has simple, broad leaves and is a common established newcomer in the UK.
Annual flowering plant believed to be native to the Middle East. It now has a worldwide distribution and grows in cultivated plots.

A variable flowering plant native across parts of Africa, much of Asia and Europe, North America and the Caribbean. It inhabits many damp or aquatic settings and bears toothed or deeply lobed leaves with small, mustard-like yellow flowers.
A rhizomatous perennial grass native to Europe, Asia and North America, it has very rough, finely toothed leaf edges sharp enough to cut skin. Its loose flower clusters have wavy, hairlike branches.

A perennial herb native to the Americas from Mexico through Central and South America to Argentina and Chile, seashore vervain has become introduced worldwide and is sometimes a noxious weed. Its rough, serrated leaves accompany upright spikes of small purple tubular flowers.

A low, hairy flowering herb native to Europe and Asia, it has creeping, much-branched stems with rounded fuzzy leaves. Its solitary, hairy, snapdragon-like flowers combine yellow, white and deep purple and have a narrow pointed spur.

An annual flowering plant native to the eastern United States and the Gulf Coast to Texas. It mainly inhabits coastal salt marshes, though a non-marine weedy variety occurs in the Ozarks. Its upright, hairless stem bears flower heads with bright yellow centres and white to lavender outer florets.
Annual thistle native to the Mediterranean Basin. Fine tangled fibres give it a cobwebbed appearance, while its rigid leaves and flower heads are sharply spiny and its florets bright yellow.

A member of the sunflower family native to the Mediterranean regions of Europe, North Africa and southwestern Asia, smooth distaff thistle is related to safflower. It is naturalized in New Zealand and California.

Wetland grass with a worldwide distribution, often forming extensive reed beds in damp ground or standing water. It bears dense dark-purple flower clusters that later look grey and silky; young shoots, sap, underground stems, seeds and other parts have documented food uses, though some are tough or scarce.
edibilityNote: Young shoots may be eaten raw or cooked; sap, underground stems, roots and seeds are also prepared as food, with some parts tough or scarce.

summary: An annual herb native to warm temperate and tropical regions of southern Eurasia and Africa. Its branching stems often spread into flat patches, while its hard fruits split into sharply spined burs capable of puncturing bicycle tyres and injuring bare feet or grazing animals.
edibilityNote: Leaves and shoots are eaten in East Asia; stems have been used to thicken diluted buttermilk.

summary: A fully submerged water plant of unstated native origin, it occurs in fresh and brackish water on every continent except Antarctica. Its very narrow leaves contain two parallel tubes, while its underground stems form starchy tubers.

Flowering grass native to southern South America, including the Pampas. It typically grows in moist soils beside waterways in its native range and is widely cultivated as an ornamental, but has become invasive in temperate regions worldwide.

A mustard plant of unstated native origin, it has cultivars grown for leafy greens, swollen stems, roots and oilseeds. Its edible leaves, seeds and stems range from peppery greens to pickles and spicy brown mustard.
edibilityNote: Leaves, seeds and stems are edible; they are eaten raw, boiled, cooked or pickled, and the seeds provide brown mustard and mustard oil.

summary: An evergreen conifer native to the eastern Mediterranean and Iran. Its dense dark-green foliage and the very narrow crown of most cultivated trees create a distinctive exclamation-mark shape. Some trees are reported to live for more than 1,000 years.
A plant found throughout the Mediterranean basin and along the European Black Sea coast. Its seed pods are edible and are foraged from March to May in Israel (Palestine).
edibilityNote: Seed pods are edible and foraged from March to May in Israel (Palestine).

summary: An upright annual flowering herb native to Eurasia, particularly most of Europe and southwestern Asia. Its dense, elongated flower spikes range from creamy white to rich crimson and appear through spring and summer.
edibilityNote: Flowers and seedling sprouts are eaten in dishes or tea and may be dried into flour; raw sprouts carry a bacterial-contamination risk.

summary: Straggly tree or mallee endemic to southern New South Wales. Its smooth bark and silvery, aromatic leaves are joined by white flowers and woody cup-shaped or cylindrical fruit. It survives in only a few scattered populations on the Central and Southern Tablelands.
Shrubby plant native to the central and eastern Mediterranean Basin. It usually has pink flowers but is very variable, and is widely grown as a decorative plant.

An evergreen fan palm believed to originate in central China, southern Japan, northern Myanmar and northern India, the Chusan palm has a rough, fibre-covered trunk and rounded fans of leaflets whose tips may be straight or drooping. Male and female flowers grow on separate trees, and the young flower buds are cooked and eaten in various ways.
edibilityNote: The young flower buds are cooked and eaten in various ways.

summary: Flowering plant native to Western Europe, including Britain and Ireland, and extending to North Africa, Italy and Greece. Its dull blue or buff-yellow flowers last only a day or so, while winter-persistent green capsules reveal scarlet seeds. Some people find that its crushed or bruised leaves have an unpleasant, beefy smell.
Small flowering herb native to Europe and Asia. Its hairy trailing stems bear widely spaced fuzzy leaves and solitary, spurred, snapdragon-like flowers patterned yellow, white and purple.

A small evergreen tree native to the American tropics. Its flowers grow in clusters directly on the trunk and older branches, while yellow-to-orange pods hold numerous seeds in white pulp. Dried, fermented seeds make cocoa and chocolate; the pulp is also used for drinks, jelly and cream.
edibilityNote: Dried, fermented seeds make cocoa and chocolate; pulp is used for juice, smoothies, jelly, cream and sometimes fermented alcoholic drinks.

summary: A flowering plant native to the southwestern highlands of Ethiopia, Arabica coffee has white flower clusters and red-to-purple “cherries” that usually contain two seeds. A drink made from its roasted seeds is recorded in historical Arab scholarship.
edibilityNote: Its roasted seeds were historically brewed as coffee, according to Arab written records.

summary: A gymnosperm tree native to East Asia, ginkgo is the last living species of an ancient plant order. Its distinctive fan-shaped leaves turn bright yellow in autumn, and some trees can live for thousands of years.
edibilityNote: Seed kernels are traditionally eaten cooked in Asian dishes, but large or prolonged intake may cause poisoning; cooking does not destroy the toxin.

summary: Woody shrub or tree native to Australia’s east coast, with outlying populations in Tasmania and on Flinders Island. It is remembered for its wrinkled grey bark, saw-toothed glossy leaves and large yellow to grey-yellow flower spikes that age into woody cones.
A sturdy perennial woody vine native to central and eastern North America. It has tiny scentless flowers and pea-sized orange fruits that are poisonous to humans when eaten.
edibilityNote: The orange fruits are poisonous to humans when ingested.

summary: A woody vine native to China, Japan and Korea. Its thin, spindly vines can climb and encircle trees, while its capsules open to reveal bright red seed coverings; all parts are poisonous.
edibilityNote: All parts of the plant are poisonous.

summary: An annual, biennial or short-lived perennial native to much of Europe, from Portugal and southern Scotland east to Ukraine and the Caucasus. Its slender stems bear deep-pink, white-spotted flowers surrounded by upright hairy bracts, and the blooms close in late afternoon.
A small flowering shrub native across much of Eurasia. Its long runners root at their tips, while its sometimes-prickly stems are bluish-grey. The black, fleshy fruits have a bluish waxy coating.
Low-growing gorse shrub native to southern Portugal, specifically the Algarve and Alentejo. Dense short hairs cover its open branches, stems and slender spines, giving the plant a silvery colour.
A small evergreen perennial native to Asia and Europe. It forms rounded mounds that can be completely covered by clear yellow flowers from mid- to late spring, though cultivars offer other colours.

A thorny tree native to Asia, with an unclear western natural limit in eastern Europe, it has silvery-scaled stems and leaves. Its aromatic creamy-yellow flowers are followed by sweet, orange-red fruit with a dry, mealy texture.
edibilityNote: The fruit is edible; dried senjed is served in syrup in an Afghan Nowruz fruit salad.

summary: A deciduous shrub or small tree native to eastern Asia from the Himalayas to Japan, autumn olive readily colonizes barren land and is invasive in parts of the United States and Europe. It often has sharp thorns, while its leaves emerge silvery and become greener above through summer. The ripe red, silver- or brown-dotted berries are sweet-tart and may be eaten fresh or made into jam, condiments or flavouring.
edibilityNote: Ripe red berries are eaten fresh or processed into jam, condiments or flavouring; they have a sweet-tart taste.

summary: A small deciduous shrub native to cool temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, it grows mainly on wet acidic soils. It has brown stems, blue-green leaves with pale net-like veins, and hanging pale-pink flowers. Its dark blue-black berries have sweet white flesh and may be eaten raw, cooked or dried.
edibilityNote: Berries are eaten raw or cooked, made into jelly, pies or infused liquor, and dried for pemmican.

summary: A small woody cycad native to the Greater Antilles, it forms low clusters with an often-underground trunk and reddish seed cones. The plant is poisonous, but the Taíno historically obtained starch from carefully leached roots and half-buried stems.
edibilityNote: The Taíno historically used carefully leached roots and half-buried stems for starch; untreated plant material is poisonous.

summary: A pine native to the New World, Pinus coulteri belongs to a group of pines distributed in Canada and the United States, excluding areas adjoining the Mexican border.

A green alga of unspecified native origin, it is distributed worldwide. Its thin, flat, translucent blades have ruffled, often torn edges and attach to rocks or other algae by a small disc. It is eaten in Scottish soups and salads and prepared in several ways in Hawaiʻi.
edibilityNote: Used in Scottish soups and salads; in Hawaiʻi, eaten mixed, salted with raw fish, boiled as soup, or served with seasonings.

summary: A green seaweed originating in the Pacific near Japan and invasive on northern Atlantic coasts. It forms dark green, velvety, finger-like branching fronds. The Atlantic subspecies is used as food in the Far East.
edibilityNote: Only Codium fragile subsp. atlanticum is documented as food in the Far East.

summary: Large deciduous tree native to northern Mexico and the southern United States around the Mississippi region. It bears nuts whose kernels are eaten raw or used in cakes and pies.
edibilityNote: The nut kernels are commonly eaten raw and used in cakes, pies and other foods.

summary: A red macroalga native to the lower intertidal coasts of the northeastern Atlantic, including Macaronesia, and the Mediterranean. It forms loose tufts of dark reddish-purple, flattened fronds, with branches that often shorten gradually toward the tips. It typically grows in tidal pools, coastal lagoons, or shallow water just below the shore.
Flowering plant native to Europe, Asia and Africa. Its small, dull-white flowers have purple tips, and its rounded fruit bears a central crest.

A succulent subtropical subshrub endemic to the western Canary Islands, it bears flattened leaf rosettes at the ends of mostly upright stems. Large pyramidal clusters of bright yellow flowers appear in spring.

A flowering shrub or small tree native to Oahu and Molokai in the Hawaiian Islands, Hibiscus arnottianus grows in tropical rainforest. Its three accepted subspecies occupy restricted parts of Oahu or eastern Molokai, and the species is assessed as endangered.

An orchid that grows on trees or rocks, native to southern China, the Himalayas and Indochina. It forms clumps of stems bearing fragrant, waxy flowers, usually in winter and spring, with colours varying from white to pink and purple.
edibilityNote: Deemed unsafe for human consumption in food supplements without a safety assessment.

summary: An herbaceous perennial native to northeastern and north-central North America, Canada goldenrod forms large colonies through spreading underground stems. Its upright growth carries branching clusters of many small yellow flowers above the foliage.
A perennial herb of damp places across the Boreal Kingdom, Ranunculus flammula flowers in June or July. It is poisonous and can be pollinated by rain.
edibilityNote: The plant is poisonous.

summary: A liverwort recorded across Europe, parts of Asia, North Africa, Madeira and North America, cliff scalewort grows mainly in damp, shady mountain habitats. Its branching plants range from light brown to dark green, appearing oily and glossy when wet but dull when dry; reproductive structures are rare.

A moss with no stated native origin, Dicranella heteromalla is widespread through the temperate Northern Hemisphere. It forms dense yellow-green to green carpets and has finely toothed leaves ending in long, sickle-curved tips that usually point to one side.

An evergreen perennial moss occurring on every continent, including Antarctica. It forms bluish-green to grey tufts on wine-red stems, and is distinguished by the long, transparent white hair at each leaf tip.
A biennial flowering plant of uncertain native origin, Alexanders has stout, hairless stems and distinctive divided leaves. Its yellow flowers help distinguish it from similar white-flowered plants.
edibilityNote: Stems are cooked like asparagus; historically, young shoots, leaves and roots were eaten fresh or cooked, especially in northern Europe and Turkey.

summary: Bearberry is a small evergreen groundcover shrub widely distributed across circumboreal regions of the subarctic Northern Hemisphere. It has shiny, thick leaves, clusters of white-to-pink flowers and bright red fruits that persist into early winter.
edibilityNote: Blackfeet people use the fruits and leaves as food; fruits may be eaten raw, made into jelly or cooked with meat, and young leaves brewed as tea.

summary: Grapevine native to eastern North America. Its berries have thick skins that slip easily from the intact pulp, while its varieties are known for pronounced strawberry, raspberry and characteristically grape-like flavours.
edibilityNote: Its grapes and derived varieties are used for wine, juice, jellies, jams, sweets and soft drinks.

summary: A coniferous tree native to the mountains of western North America, white fir has flattened green to blue-green needles. Its green or purple cones ripen pale brown, then disintegrate to release winged seeds about six months after pollination. It can live for more than 300 years.

A shrub or small tree native to the western United States, western juniper usually grows on dry, rocky mountain sites. It bears blue-brown, berry-like cones with a whitish bloom; some Oregon distilleries use these cones to flavour gin.
edibilityNote: Berry-like cones have been used by some Oregon distilleries to flavour gin.

summary: A large evergreen conifer native to the west coast of North America, Sitka spruce is the largest spruce species and can exceed 100 metres in height. It has stiff, sharp blue-green needles and thin, scaly bark.
edibilityNote: New branch tips are used to flavour spruce beer or boiled for syrup, while the needles can be made into aromatic tea.

summary: A flowering perennial native to eastern Africa from Kenya to Mozambique, it has abundant spurred flowers and ripe seedpods that burst open. Its soft stems, leaves, flowers and roots are easily damaged.

A perennial flowering plant native to China, Japan and Korea, it spreads on thin red runners that form new plantlets. Its white flowers have two petals noticeably longer than the other three, and its foliage is occasionally eaten fresh or cooked in Japanese cuisine.
edibilityNote: The foliage is occasionally used fresh or cooked in Japanese cuisine.

summary: A deciduous tree native from China through Southeast Asia to the Indian subcontinent, the orchid tree bears conspicuous pink or white flowers. Its mature pods twist into corkscrews and burst open with an audible clack. In South Asia, its edible buds are cooked in curries, stir-fried or pickled, while flowers and buds make Nepalese pickles.
edibilityNote: Buds are cooked in curries, stir-fried or pickled across South Asia; flowers and buds are used in Nepalese pickles.

summary: A perennial moss found on every continent, including Antarctica. Its grey-green leaves have reddish-brown tips and spread wider when moist; it commonly grows on dry, acidic, exposed ground.

A moss widely distributed through temperate and boreal parts of the Northern Hemisphere, common haircap moss also occurs in Mexico, several Pacific islands and Australia. Exceptionally tall for a moss, it usually grows in bogs, wet heathland and beside forest streams; its leaves curve and twist around the stem when conditions become too dry.

Moss with a worldwide distribution outside most tropical areas, growing on wet soil and rocks around streams, lakes, fens and marshes. Its glossy young leaves become dull red-brown with age, extend strongly down the stem and twist when dry.

A deciduous tropical tree native to parts of tropical Asia and Oceania, it bears red, five-petalled flowers in spring before new leaves appear. Its ripe seed capsules contain white cotton-like fibres, while the trunk bears spikes, especially when young.
edibilityNote: Flowers are dried and cooked in Myanmar; dried flower cores flavour Thai soups and curry, and flower-bud calyxes were historically eaten in India.

summary: A flowering plant native to tropical Africa from Sudan to the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Mozambique, and to Saudi Arabia and Yemen. It is sometimes planted in butterfly gardens.

An epiphytic flowering plant native to the Philippines. It anchors in debris collected in tree forks and bears long clusters of pink, red or violet flowers with pink bracts, followed by fleshy violet berries.
